subsubtopic: USE OF GOVERNMENT AIRCRAFT BY PRIME MINISTER-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to request consent of the House to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity arising out of the continued use of government-owned aircraft by the Prime Minister for personal and political purposes at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada. I ask leave of the House to move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):
That the House requests the Prime Minister to discontinue immediately making any use whatsoever of government-owned aircraft for personal or political purposes, and further that the House requests the government to bill the Liberal Party of Canada for the political portion of transportation costs arising in the past few days from the Prime Minister's use of government-owned aircraft for a trip that included certain Liberal Party gatherings, including the annual meeting of the Ontario Liberal Party in Sudbury.

subsubtopic: LAG IN INCREASE IN WEEKLY WAGES COMPARED WITH INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the Minister of Finance and bring home to him once again the deplorable situation of the average Canadian wage earner in that, although the average wage has increased by 8 per cent or $12.53 from February, 1973, to February, 1974, the consumer price index has risen by 9.6 per cent or $15.02, or a difference of $3.51. What is the minister's response to these recent indices indicating that average weekly wages con-

tinue to lag behind the rising cost of living? What response does the government have to deal with this situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: LAG IN INCREASE IN WEEKLY WAGES COMPARED WITH INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to express my continuing concern about the situation the hon. gentleman has described in terms of the real income of Canadian workers. The response I might make might be more fully digested within the budget speech a week from today. I want to bring to the hon. member's attention that many of the yardsticks used in the statistical form purportedly showing a decrease in labour income do, in a sense, distort the situation in that they do not allow for the changed mix in the labour force, for the increase in hourly as against weekly wages, and for the decline in the average work week. This is a statistical matter which I should like to deal with in more general terms on another occasion.

Relocation of Railway Lines

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some comments about some matters which have not been raised in questions to the minister. There are a number of small municipalities which may have railways running through their boundaries but which may not be able to raise enough capital to cover their share of railway line relocation. My first comment is that the bill does not go far enough in providing assistance for those smaller communities. To illustrate my concern, I might use Wetaski-win as an example. Wetaskiwin, a community of approximately 6,500 people, is not unlike other cities of the same size in Canada. Over the years the people of Wetaskiwin have become increasingly concerned because the two CPR main lines, and especially the yard in the middle of the city, have created a hazard and inconvenience for pedestrians, vehicular traffic and vehicles performing a public service which need to cross the tracks.
The lines were built about 75 years ago to provide a rail link between Calgary and Edmonton. Over the years, because the city has grown and society has become more automated, the residents of Wetaskiwin have been forced to attempt to correct the increasingly undesirable railway crossing situation.
In 1969 the city of Wetaskiwin carried out a study concerning the main problems created by the CPR lines. The study concluded, first, that slow moving potash trains disrupt movement of traffic from either side of the railway tracks for periods between 20 and 32 minutes at a time. Second, that serious inconvenience is caused to pedestrian traffic, and extreme discomfort, during the inclement weather of the winter months. Pedestrians have even been observed climbing between the railways cars. A high degree of danger has existed at all crossings in the morning, at noon and in the afternoon owing to the student population of three schools using the crossings. Third, when an alarm was given, the effectiveness of fire hall equipment located on the west side of the Canadian Pacific tracks, and fire protection to the east side of the city where the major industrial development is, was reduced to nil. Officials of Canadian Pacific advised that it was impossible to break up or separate a slow-moving train in case of an emergency. They said that separating it would take approximately as long as allowing the train to clear the crossing.
The fourth finding of the study was that the effectiveness of police protection, emergency medical and ambulance service was also reduced to nil during the passage over the crossings of the aforementioned trains.
That, basically, is the problem facing the good people of Wetaskiwin as well as the people of many other small communities.
Wetaskiwin has taken a serious approach to solving its rail relocation problems, despite obvious financial restraints placed on it because of its size. I have a copy of a detailed engineering study of the rail relocation situation which was undertaken by the city of Wetaskiwin. If Bill C-27 as drafted is passed, Wetaskiwin's concern about this problem probably has all been for naught, as it is not financially able to pay for 50 per cent of the cost of relocation.
The estimated cost of the Wetaskiwin rail relocation project is $2.5 million. The city, perhaps, can spend $400,-

000 or approximately 25 per cent of its annual budget on this project, but that is a far cry from the $1.25 million it would be required to pay if the legislation as drafted is passed.
The government might reconsider the financial aspects of the proposed legislation, for the sake of Wetaskiwin and for the sake of all small and medium sized communities across Canada which desperately need rail lines to be relocated but cannot afford to do so. Does the minister consider that Bill C-27 provides for sufficient capitalization for small communities, so that they will not be financially burdened? They are not asking for $35 million or $50 million. However, it is necessary for them to come up with some money to carry out such projects as I have suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member raised several proposals regarding Wetaskiwin. I do not think he would expect me to reply in detail to those, as there are about 64 applications of various sorts before the CTC, including that of Wetaskiwin. That city has outlined to the CTC the railroad relocation project it wishes to see undertaken.
May I say two things to the hon. member. First, Wetaskiwin obviously will fall under the purview of this act. Clearly, it is an urban area as defined in this legislation. The hon. member referred to the difficulty of school children crossing the track in order to go to school. May I refer him to the provisions on page 20 of the bill which cover pedestrian crossings. It will be possible to build pedestrian crossings, to correct the situation the hon. member mentioned.
I may be mistaken, but I thought the hon. member mentioned that the cost of the project in his city would be $250 million.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: No. $2.5 million.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
That is more appropriate, as a $250 million project would be more expensive than any proposed rail relocation project in Canada, including that of Winnipeg which, depending on the options decided on, may cost about $75 million.
With regard to whether under the legislation we would cover half the cost of the relocation, I caution the hon. member that the figure $2.5 million may well be simply the cost of removing the railway facilities without taking into account the net benefit to the railways provided by the relocation, which would be subtracted from that cost for purposes of the legislation.
Under this legislation, when we have a railroad relocation proposal and railroads are moved from one area to the other, this is done without cost or benefit. There would be real benefit in many railroad relocations which are put on to the ledger. Therefore, I caution the hon. member about using the gross figure, which is simply the cost of moving the railroad without taking into account the net benefits provided for in the legislation.
In answer to the hon. member's larger question about whether there is sufficient capital, obviously any government or any minister would like to say we have more money and we could spend more money. It is easy to spend
April 29, 1974

more money. We have a formula here which provides 50 per cent of the cost of railroad relocation, and obviously people can argue it should be more.
I would hope to see the provinces and municipalities assist in relocation schemes. They should assist. In Saskatchewan, for example, it seems appropriate that the Saskatchewan government make a contribution toward the relocation. Fifty per cent is spelled out in the legislation as the federal contribution. The other parties, be they the province, city or the railroads themselves, can make up the balance of 50 per cent. Obviously my answer to the hon. member is yes, we could use more money, but within any government we have to exercise priorities as to the amount of money available or as to the formula set out to pay for the undertaking.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for his extensive answer. I hope we do not scare the Wetaskiwin residents out of their wits with a figure of $250 million. Am I correct in assuming that under the terms of the bill, after the rail tracks are relocated the land becomes the property of the federal Department of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in 99 per cent of the cases that will not happen. However, to give this bill any teeth, you have to put into it the power of the CTC to have the final say that something should happen. It is given the power to order that a relocation be conducted. It is given additional power to order, if it is necessary to carry out the plan, that the federal Minister of Public Works expropriate the railroad land. However, he would do so purely as a trustee for the end result or benefit of the plan. He would expropriate solely for the purpose of being a conduit. He would acquire the land from the railroad, being the only person in Canada authorized to expropriate railroad property, as a trustee in accordance with the plan and pass it on to the province, municipality or private interests that are designed within the plan to acquire and use this railroad land. He acquires it solely as a trustee.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Is it correct to say the city could then become owner of part of this land to offset the cost of its 50 per cent of the relocation?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, it would not, because the net costs of relocation would be worked out. We would pay 50 per cent of those net costs. It would then be determined where the balance of the 50 per cent comes from. The municipality could, of course, acquire part of the railway land, and in some cases they will, but that would be put into the equation of the cost of the scheme. It is not a way by which they could acquire the land for nothing.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
The small communities will have a hard time finding half the capital that is required. However, if they could have assurance that part of the land the railway is vacating in the middle of the city could become city property, it could then recover some of the original capital it had to come up with for its 50 per cent. It would make it much easier for cities to relocate their rail lines if they could be assured that at least some of the land would revert to the city, for sale to private interests as well as for

parks, future rapid transit or whatever happens to come forward.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that under the plan the city involved could acquire all or any part of the railroad land if that was part of the urban development plan. I thought the hon. member was referring to that as a method of acquiring the land for nothing. That they could not do. However, they could acquire the land as part of the urban development plan for disposal or use for some other purpose. There is no question about that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Wetaskiwin permit me to enter into discussion at this point?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very intrigued by the minister's answers to the questions raised by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. Has the minister a legal opinion from the Department of Justice as to the ownership of the land underneath the rails? I put my question another way by saying that under the charter of the CPR and under the charter of the various railways that make up the CNR, this land belonged to the Crown and was granted to these railways for the sole purpose of transportation. When any railway gives up land and no longer uses it for the purpose for which the charter was granted, all that land beneath the rails reverts to the Crown, which was the grantee. Has he a legal opinion on that?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, ministers are not supposed to give legal opinions. I will make some inquiries about the point. In any event, I do not think it affects the operation or wording of this particular legislation because the expropriation section provides that the Minister of Public Works is authorized to acquire by way of expropriation land that is or was occupied as part of the railway undertaking by the company. The legal consequences of that expropriation, I suggest, would flow from that statement.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that was not my question. I did not ask the minister for a legal opinion. I asked whether he had had one given to him by the officials of the Department of Justice. If he would ask for that legal opinion and read those charters again, the Justice officials would probably rule that the land underneath the rails, once it is no longer used for railroad purposes, reverts to the Crown. Therefore, it is impossible to expropriate something you already own. This is the reason I asked the question. The minister said that approximately 99 per cent of the land comes back to the Crown and the other 1 per cent does not.
This brings me to my second question. In the case of the railways taking the railway lines out of the cities of Calgary and Saskatoon, did the railways not assume that the land they had vacated in those cities belonged to them and through real estate development made a large sum of money in compensation for that sale? In the case of Calgary, I think it was over $100 million. What has been the past experience of the railways and those dealing with them concerning claims to the land beneath the right of

Relocation of Railway Lines
way-the rail lines abandoned in Saskatoon, Calgary and elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: On a point of information, I wish to correct one thing. It is my impression the hon. member said we would be using this power of expropriation in 99 per cent of these cases. In fact, we envisage expropriation as a means of implementing relocation being used in only a minority of cases. In the vast majority of cases the process will be handled by agreement and negotiation. While we trust the process can be implemented without expropriations, we do, obviously, feel it is essential that such power should be conferred under the act. The CTC has power to order the relocation of rail lines in certain areas. Under the formula to determine the net cost of relocation, the railroads are, among other things, credited with the value of the land that is vacated as part of the net cost of the scheme. Whether they end up by owning it or not will depend on a particular scheme, but obviously it will be shown as an asset of the companies.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
I did not
misunderstand the minister; the figure of 99 per cent came from him, and I am in agreement. I should like to complete my questioning by asking the minister whether he would refer the question of the ownership of these rights of way to the legal officers of the Department of Justice. To whom does the right of way belong once the railway has abandoned the track? The answer may well be that the land reverts to the Crown. If this is the case, I should like an opinion from these legal officers as to who owns land in country areas, in similar circumstances when a line has been abandoned. There are miles of abandoned line along rights of way in areas which are not covered by the present bill. Do the railways claim ownership of this land or not? Or does it revert to the Crown? I believe the legal position will be that the land does revert to the Crown, in which case why should we credit the railways with the value of land in this limited area involving cities? The land belongs to the people.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the proposal here is to expropriate not only the right of way but the land which physically affords the right of way. The hon. member began his question by talking about mineral rights. That is an altogether different thing. What is involved here is the right of way, a right to put tracks down and surface rights. This is the subject of the claim to ownership. It is certainly the view of the railway companies that they own not only the tracks on the right of way but the land the right of way covers.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
That is the point at issue. It is clear the minister considers they own the surface rights and the land along these tracks. I never mentioned mineral rights. I am dealing only with surface rights. I wish the minister would go to the legal advisers and ask them for an opinion, for an interpretation of the original charters concerning land granted to the railways, and whether this land along the rights of way belongs to the Crown when the railways, of their own volition, or on the direction of the Commission, abandon those lines. Do the surface rights revert to the Crown? I

know the minister cannot answer that question until he has referred it to the legal advisers of the Crown.
Will the minister also tell us what he can about the disposition of the land in Saskatoon, Calgary, and in other cities from which the railways voluntarily removed the tracks? It is possible there is a debt still owing to the Crown. To whom was the value of the land credited?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
We shall apply the legislation and expropriate only where we need to do so and in connection with land which the railways own. If it is held legally that the railways do not own the surface rights once the tracks are abandoned, then obviously this would be a matter for settlement by litigation. We certainly do not intend to expropriate rights which do not exist.
I must say, with regard to voluntarily relocation schemes, that I am not familiar with the two schemes to which the hon. member referred. In the case of the scheme which was put into effect in the national capital area the railway companies undoubtedly took the position that they owned the right of way and the surface rights. These were acquired by the National Capital Commission after payment of very substantial amounts to the railway companies as part of the cost of the relocation scheme.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: That is the point I am making, Mr. Chairman. There is evidence that the railways have taken the position that they own the surface rights in respect of the land beneath the rails. I accept the minister's assurance that he will ask for a legal opinion as to who owns the surface rights in the circumstances I have mentioned, those rights having been given to the railways by charter for a specific purpose.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the question which has just been raised by my hon. friend is a very important one from the point of view of the smaller communities. It would be much easier for them to bear the 50 per cent of the cost if they could get back an interest in at least part of these lands and, possibly, dispose of them commercially.
The point I wish to raise has to do with the amount of funds designated under this program. If Winnipeg takes $50 million and other major cities have budgets of a similar size-I do not know how many millions Toronto will need-there will only be a limited opportunity for the smaller cities to participate. Can the minister assure us that at least part of this money will be set aside to meet the needs of the smaller communities?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to make it clear that schemes such as the Winnipeg scheme which carry a high price tag do not exhaust the budget. It would be wrong to take $75 million for Winnipeg and assume, on that basis, that most of the money in the fund has been expended. Such schemes will take many years to complete, perhaps as long as ten years, and the budget would be spread over that period.
I might also say that the CTC is authorized to make rules and set priorities in connection with relocation plans. I can only express my hope that the CTC, having been given a certain degree of independence by the government, will deal not only with major centres when setting priorities but will also set some in respect of

smaller parts of the country. In terms of ministerial assurance, I can say to the hon. member that I think the allocation of government of Canada funds should be made on a somewhat fair and equitable basis.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, like many who have participated in this debate on this measure I should like to add my words of congratulation to the minister and indicate that we certainly welcome this measure presently before us.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
I appreciate that applause. I was beginning to despair that we would never see this legislation brought before parliament; when I have raised questions on a number of occasions in the past the reply was always that this legislation would be brought in a very short time, or in several weeks, or that we could expect to have it before the House very soon. Now, a year and a half after it was predicted that this measure would be before us, we are looking forward to finding out some of the details relating to its operation.
A number of questions have been raised since the bill was introduced, and, while the minister has replied to some of them, there are still some that require clarification.
In reply to a question I raised about the Chilliwack situation some time ago the minister indicated he was aware of the particular problem and had discussed it. I have already expressed through the news media in my area my appreciation for the commitment the minister has made, but I very much regret that this was done on a basis that gave rise to some serious questions of a political nature. That was very unfortunate and I do not think the minister really intended that it should come out in that fashion. In any event that is the way it happened. However, that does not detract from my appreciation for the announcement of this measure.
Having regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, who spoke about the measure as it relates to smaller communities in his area, there are two small areas in my riding that are vitally concerned with this bill. One is Chilliwack, to which I have referred, and the other is Abbotsford, both major points of population in my section of the country.
This bill proposes the expenditure of $250 million over a period of five years for track relocation. I should like to raise the same question raised by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin as to what assurance the minister can give that the smaller communities in Canada, such as those to which I have referred, along with many others, will receive the benefit of this measure. There are a number of cities which I understand have major projects on the drawing board. As has been pointed out, these will involve a considerable outlay of capital. My concern is that the major part, if not all, of these funds will be taken up by the major population areas and the smaller areas will not be able to qualify. It almost seems that many of the areas will be classed as rural and, therefore, will not have the opportunity to participate at all.
Relocation of Railway Lines
Let me point out first that not only in the majoi areas but also in the smaller urban centres there are major problems in respect to trackage. One to which 1 wish to refer is in the city of Chilliwack, which is divided by the CNR main line. Their major services such as police, ambulance and transportation to the airport are seriously hampered by railway traffic. I believe Chilliwack has outlined a very sound proposal which involves moving the tracks. I should like to ask whether this measure applies strictly to urban areas. In this particular case part of the relocation suggested would be in the urban area, but part would also involve tracks in the rural area adjacent to the city. If this bill applies strictly to urban areas, I think there will be serious difficulty in working out this program.
This program should not be retained for the benefit only of urban areas. A great deal of discussion has taken place in the last while about the quality of rural life, about making it more attractive to many people who have an appreciation for that kind of life by providing them with a certain quality of amenities, and so on. If we are going to help the rural areas we must look at this program as it applies to them. In order to make rural life even more attractive perhaps some of these rail tracks should be moved to other sections.
When speaking to one of the mayors in my community just over the week end he voiced the suggestion and belief that the time had come when there must be transportation corridors instead of chopping up the country according to sections. He suggested there should be corridors in which all communications facilities could be located. This is one of the things that should be considered in light of the measure currently before the committee.
Let me refer to another matter which might go beyond the reference of this bill. I have received a number of communications regarding a coal dust situation adjacent to our rail lines. This subject perhaps comes within the jurisdiction of the Minister of the Environment, but since we are discussing rail transportation and the responsibility of rail companies to communities and community living, I think this matter should be considered now.
In spite of the fact there have been a number of studies, a great many communications and an extensive lapse of time, these companies do not seem to have come up with any solution to this coal dust problem. I suppose this problem affects major areas as well where rail lines pass through areas of concentrated population. These people are subject to a great deal of pollution which the railways should have some responsibility to correct.
This minister as well as the Minister of the Environment and others engaged in or having some influence in this particular area should lend their weight and prestige to the finding of a solution to this coal dust problem. This may involve relocating the tracks in some areas, and this certainly should be considered within the terms of reference of this bill.
There is one other point I should like to raise, and this relates to the principle of a 50-50 division of cost. It does not seem that the railways are to assume any responsibility for this particular project, that this is all going to be done by the government. In view of the fact that the railway companies have gained considerably as a result of government co-operation in the past, possibly they should
April 29, 1974

Relocation of Railway Lines
be called upon to bear some of the cost of relocating these tracks, particularly if this is to be for the benefit of the communities, their further development and their general standard of living.
Perhaps these companies should be called upon to pay 10 per cent, 15 per cent or 20 per cent of the relocation costs, as this would make them a little bit more responsible in respect of some of these areas of concern.
Those are just a few of the thoughts I would raise. There is this matter of allocation of funds and recognizing the legitimate claims of smaller communities, even some that are classified rural. This is one of the major concerns of a great many people in this country, and certainly of a great many people in my particular area.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I just respond very briefly to the hon. member by assuring him that while we may like to think of urban areas as referring to Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, the definition of "urban" within this act is a very wide one. In fact, it covers all of the populated areas in Canada. Without question it would cover the cities of Chilliwack and Abbotsford to which the hon. member referred in that, for one purpose of the definition, it is any municipality with a population of 1,000 or more people having the legal status of a city, town or village. So there is no question that the centres within the hon. member's riding would be covered by the Statistics Canada definition. However, the point he makes is a good one and we have put forward a definition which will cover all the populated areas in Canada.
Second, I refer the hon. member to the fact that what many of the smaller towns and villages of this country need is not a railway relocation proposal but an underpass or an overpass on the railroad's track itself. That is covered by Parts II and III of the bill which make no distinction between urban and rural. So the cities he refers to could take advantage of Part I in the railroad relocation proposals and, without question, take advantage of Parts II and III for the construction of grade crossings, underpasses and that type of work.
I appreciate the hon. member raising those concerns and I think that we have tried to respond to them in this legislation.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to comment on this bill for a few moments. First, I should like to join my colleagues who have already congratulated the government, particularly the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, for finally bringing forward Bill C-27. It is difficult not to agree with the bill whose stated purpose is to facilitate the relocation of railway lines, particularly at a time when the redesigning and reconstruction of our major cities is so much a matter of concern to those of us who have the honour of representing large urban centres.
However, I must express a concern which I feel rather personally. It stems from the fact that, while we welcome this legislation, we cannot help but be concerned about ensuring that the government does carry forward its promises with some degree of efficiency and speed. Having regard to the responsibilities that are incumbent

upon a government introducing such major legislation, speed is, of course, a matter of concern.
I think that a measure of any department's efficiency and concern for people's problems is shown to a member of parliament when he deals with a particular department on behalf of a constituent. Because here you have a small matter affecting an individual person whose member of parliament has decided to contact a minister responsible for a department to see what can be done on behalf of that individual citizen.
With regard to the Department of State for Urban Affairs, I must say to the minister that I cannot be overly confident about the manner in which his department will proceed with the implementation of this bill on the basis of my personal experience in making representations on behalf of a particular constituent. I wrote to the minister on behalf of a Mr. Dean Knowles on February 19 of this year, and have yet to receive an acknowledgement or a substantive reply in any form. On March 26, over a month having passed, I sent the minister a copy of a letter I had sent to my constituent indicating that no reply as yet had been received. Still no acknowledgement or response was received by me. Last Thursday, in fairness to the department and to the minister, I decided to call his office to see if the correspondence had been mislaid. I was told by a secretary there that they prided themselves on the efficiency and speed with which they dealt with correspondence. She said that the correspondence would be checked and that an assistant to the minister would telephone me back. That call never came.
So, having listened to the congratulations of other hon. members, I join with them with regard to the specific legislation, but I have to express concern that my own personal experience in making representations on behalf of constituents does not give me much confidence with regard to the efficiency with which this minister will implement this piece of legislation.
This legislation interests me in particular, coming as I do from the great city of Hamilton, because, as do other urban centres, we welcome it. The city of Hamilton is served by the CNR, the CPR and another railway called the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo railway. So we have more than our share of railway lines. Both because we are serviced by them and because we are an industrial city, this type of relocation will be something we welcome and can certainly use.
I think it is important to note that what we are talking about is not the removal of railway lines, but their relocation because they are still needed. In addition to the cost factor involved in such a move, we should be taking a very close look at what the environmental and social effects of relocating these railway lines will be. You cannot simply solve a problem by relocating the particular cause of it to another area, not expecting some other type of problem to be caused in the area where those lines are relocated. In a city that is industrial, that accepts some of the disadvantages along with many of the advantages of being an industrial city, we have a right to expect of this ministry a full study into the environmental and social impact of any move before such move takes place.
I also hope that the ultimate decision will be made at the local level. Because in looking at this piece of legislation
April 29, 1974

we see that at least three ministries, the Department of State for Urban Affairs, the Ministry of Transport and the Department of Public Works, will be involved in its implementation. If there is one thing we do not need any more in this country it is a continuation of or an addition to the process of decision making by bureaucrats in Ottawa which affects people in Wetaskiwin, Hamilton, Vancouver, Montreal, and in many other places. We have much too much of that already, we do not need any more of it. If this legislation is to be effective, then the ultimate decisions will have to be made at the local level.
I noted with interest that some city mayors, including His Worship the Mayor of Hamilton, were in Ottawa not so long ago to request funds of the federal government. This legislation, which does assist cities, is a step in the right direction. We must be moving in these times toward giving more financial assistance to the cities. I recognize that under our system of government the federal government has a perfect, tailor-made excuse when it says: "We cannot give money directly to municipalities; we must deal through the provinces". If that is the case, so be it. But let it deal with them through the provinces. Our municipalities are so large, they have to carry so many services, and their base for revenue is so small in comparison with that of the federal and provincial governments, that it is incumbent upon all these levels of government to join together in programs for better revenue sharing such as the one in Bill C-27 and the one that was brought in in the United States not so long ago, whereby the federal government can assist to a much greater extent the large urban centres.
I am also concerned about the substantial power which has been given to the Canadian Transport Commission. Again based on my personal experience and knowledge of this branch of the government I cannot have great confidence in the CTC. They are simply too powerful and their jurisdiction too centralized.
If we are going to have any degree of success with this legislation, then in addition to consultation we must have co-ordination. This is something the CTC does not seem to know exists or, if it does know, it shies away from it. That is a concern I wish to register with the minister.
About nine months ago the Minister of Transport claimed that Canada's total transportation system "represents perhaps one of the best, if not the best, in the world." But earlier this year he changed his mind and described Canada's transportation system as being in a mess. What he clearly admitted is that Canada does not have a real transportation policy. Such a policy was promised, but it does not exist.
If the government goes ahead with its grandiose plans and schemes, however well intentioned, they cannot succeed unless we have a co-ordinated and unified transportation system. The best intentions of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs will fall by the wayside because of the lack of a transportation policy and because of the mess that exists in the Department of Transport.
Every day in the House of Commons the Minister of Transport is questioned about what the government's plans will be for such things as the future of the railroads,
Relocation of Railway Lines
particularly in the west, and about the government's decisions in regard to airports. We simply do not know, Mr. Chairman, and the people affected do not know. I believe we should be taking a definite look now at the whole future of railroads in Canada because, as my colleague from Central Nova pointed out in the latter part of last week, a survey has been conducted which is not very encouraging to those of us who wish to place reliability in our railroad transportation system.
The "Modernization of Railways in Canada", a survey completed by the engineering faculty of Carleton University, reveals that utilization of railways in Canada and levels of investment are similar to those of other industrialized nations, but that passenger rail service performance in Canada is far below that of other countries.
It also reveals that although technologies superior to those in Canada have been developed for traction, suspension, track construction and traffic control, the manning of Canadian railways is still based on the steam tradition and does not allow efficient operation of modern equipment. In effect, it says that Canada's railways compared with those of other countries are slow, are usually not on time, and are unsafe particularly when the weather is bad. It also refers to statistics which show that our railway lines, compared with those of other countries, are not as sage, and in fact are becoming more dangerous.
A special inquiry into railway safety, commissioned by the Canadian Transport Commission, reported last December that the number of derailments caused by poor track conditions on both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways in 1972 was three times that of 1959, and nearly double that of 1969, despite the fact that improved technology with respect to mechanical means of transportation is at our disposal.
Obviously, if anything is to be done about this matter the leadership must come from the federal government. And leadership must come in a co-ordinated fashion, not just from the Minister of State for Urban Affairs but from the Minister of Transport, co-ordinating all the different ministries and programs that are concerned with these matters.
I have already mentioned concern for safety on our railways. My concern also extends to pedestrians and travellers in cars. One of the reasons for the relocation of tracks from major urban centres is to provide a greater measure of safety, particularly in a city like Hamilton where the tracks cross main thoroughfares, endangering the lives of pedestrians and car travellers.
In a particular instance in the city of Hamilton, a railway crossing located in a high density population area has been a hazard for some time, and in fact has already claimed one life. At the urging of the aldermen for the area we arranged a meeting with CTC representatives from Ottawa to show them how this railway line was endangering the lives of the young school children and apartment dwellers in that area of east Hamilton. We urged that if they could not relocate the line immediately-something which may be possible following passage of this bill-in the meantime they should provide the maximum amount of protection possible for pedestrians and people riding in cars.

But the CTC hid behind its big rule book and pointed out that since there was only one railway track involved, not two, there was no requirement that safety guards be placed there. Mr. Chairman, many urban areas simply cannot afford to provide the full protection that is necessary at crossing levels, and the CTC should assist them so that they may buy the necessary equipment. Such equipment could then be removed and used elsewhere once a particular rail line had been relocated in a safer place.
I hope the minister will comment on the possibility of taking such a suggestion into consideration, and will also let us know what he has in mind under Bill C-27 for the city of Hamilton. As I have already mentioned to him, those of us who have the pleasure of living in Hamilton have a particular concern about railway lines. Indeed, we may have more than our share of them. We would like to know what information he can provide us with with respect to the benefit that the city of Hamilton can expect from implementation of this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has raised several matters. I find his reference to correspondence with my office shocking and disturbing, because I have a rule that correspondence must be answered within ten days. I have already sent off an inquiry to find out what is involved in the situation to which he refers.
The hon. member also said that in any relocation scheme environmental and ecological considerations must be taken into account. I agree with him. As the legislation provides, before the CTC can act an urban development plan must be laid before it, and I find it inconceivable that any such plan would be drawn up without taking into account the ecological and environmental aspects of the proposed relocation scheme.
The hon. member was also concerned about the application process and the cost sharing formula. He will note from Part I of the bill that any relocation or rerouting proposal will require the closest degree of intergovernmental consultation and co-operation. As we see it, the urban development plan and the transportation plan will be drawn up at the initiation of the municipality or province involved. It will be referred to the CTC with comments on any federal programs that my ministry is involved in to ensure co-ordination, and the Department of Transport will concern itself with the transportation aspects of any relocation. I think in this legislation we have tried to provide for good interdepartmental and intergovernmental consultation and co-ordination.
The hon. member referred to the Canadian Transport Commission. Their role is provided for in the legislation for obvious reasons: they are the regulatory agency at the federal level with jurisdiction over railroads, railroad rights of way and railroad activities. I think the hon. member will agree that it would have been wrong to set up another federal regulatory body to deal solely with railroad relocation.
I agree with the hon. member on the point he and a number of other members raised, namely that the municipalities, the provinces, members of parliament and the government are entitled to expect the CTC to operate

efficiently and effectively and with speed when dealing with applications. Several hon. members have said that the CTC needs a good shaking up. I believe we are entitled to expect it to deal with applications made under Part I in an effective and an efficient manner, and I think the Minister of Transport can be relied upon to ensure that this will be done.
With regard to questions of safety, I would refer hon. members to Part II and III of the bill. Part II provides for special expenses for grade crossings and grade separation schemes, and Part III provides for amendments to the grade crossing fund, doubling-and I am speaking loosely-the federal contributions to grade crossings and grade separations.
The removal of grade crossings has made an important contribution to safety. Statistics show that while automobile accidents have increased over the last few years, the percentage of automobile accidents at grade crossings has decreased. This is largely the result of safety work at level crossings and also the large numbers of grade separations that have been constructed.
The amendments to Parts II and III, which allow the CTC and the grade crossing fund to work on a great many more safety features at level crossings by way of safety devices, also allow for the building of more grade separations, and thus make an important contribution to safety.
I am not familiar with the case referred to by the hon. member as I am not responsible for the grade crossing fund, but I will give instructions that this be looked into. I do not understand why action was not taken because there was only one track and not two.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I cannot say what the particular plans are for Hamilton under this legislation, but knowing the leadership of that city and the representation it has in this House I am sure the case will be put very effectively and vigorously before the CTC. Indeed, if we are not very careful Hamilton will manage to get the bulk of any moneys provided under this legislation.
Lastly, Mr. Chairman, I can advise the hon. member that with regard to the first point that he raised about the mortgage dispute of a Mr. Knowles, this does require extensive research by CMHC but the hon. member will be getting a letter from me tonight.

Mr. Chairman, I must apologize for not being quite as well prepared as I might be. I was forced to be away from the House last week and, unfortunately, have not had a chance to study this legislation.
Belleville, the major city in my riding, has for many years considered that the CPR tracks running through it should be removed. It is fair to say that, even if the majority of the residents favour the removal of the track, the official town plan and the revision do not speak at length of removing these tracks, because for many years this course has been thought of as being too expensive. Seven or eight years ago when I was mayor of Belleville I discussed with senior officials of the CPR the possibility of moving these tracks. They felt this would be possible, although the cost was prohibitive. The railway would not undertake the removal, and the city could not afford to do it as the cost of removing the track was equal to the entire city budget for one year.
The tracks traverse the entire south boundary of the city, right along the shore of the beautiful Bay of Quinte. History says that the CPR forced that particular track location on the city. I would not say the city was blackmailed, but the city fathers were told that if they wanted
Relocation of Railway Lines
to be served by the railway the rail lines would need to run along the waterfront. We can understand the reasoning behind that. As the railway was necessary for the development of the community and industry, which in those days tended to locate along the waterfront for reasons of easy access, it did not seem unreasonable to build the tracks on that valuable property.
As the years went by the city grew to the north. The Montreal-Toronto CNR railings bisect the city. Citizens accepted that development as reasonable. There are, across the CP tracks at the south end of the city, seven or eight level crossings. Despite many of these being equipped with signals-some are just now being so equipped-there was this past winter an unfortunate death at one of these crossings. So the removal of these tracks or their relocation would make life safer for the people in the city. It would protect them and would be a convenience. Once the tracks are gone, property values in the area would increase, and that would help the city coffers. If it were not for the tracks, some of that land would be the most valuable in the city. Its value will be greatly enhanced by the removal of the tracks.
I should point out that the tracks run north of the city on the west and on the east, and only dip down to the south as they go through the city. So the physical relocation would not be unreasonable. Some provision would need to be made for those industries which would remain in the south end of the city until they wished to move. In the interim those industries would need to be protected.
I wish to ask the minister some questions. As I say, I have not digested the legislation thoroughly; I only looked at it briefly this afternoon, after returning to Ottawa, I am somewhat concerned about the cost of the preparation of an urban development plan. Clause 3(1) and 3(5) provide for such plans to be presented. There is provision for their enactment, after proper study. That is, the plans can be carried out. The bill provides for cost sharing and goes into detail as to how such plan is to be implemented. However, I do not see any provision allowing for the application for such study.
I note the words in the recommendation of His Excellency calling for not more than 50 per cent of the cost of urban development plans and transportation studies to be paid. I would be most surprised if the city of Belleville does not almost immediately ask for assistance to study this subject in detail. Of course, whether it could afford to carry out the proposed relocation would depend on the result of the study. This question has been in the minds of the mayor, members of council and many citizens for a long time, and they would be most interested in knowing how the city could apply for assistance for undertaking a study.
I will ask the minister some questions, wait for him to reply, then perhaps think of some more questions which may clarify this matter in my mind.
Having been mayor of Belleville and having had to deal with both CN and CP, I have learned several things about the railways. The CNR is a major employer in Belleville; at one time it was the major employer. Its importance as an employer has lessened somewhat, but it still is a major employer.

The CPR lines run through the city but the company is not as physical visible as the CNR is. Having dealt with the railways from time to time, I have found that CN and CP argue quite a bit and that the spirit of co-operation between them does not exist in the way we think it should. May I ask the minister if, in his opinion, the railways will be invited to participate in the planning of any relocation?
When I was mayor of Belleville we removed an anachronism of Southern Ontario, that portion of railway line which had run down the second main street of Belleville for many years. We finally got rid of it. Frankly, co-operation between the two railways was not evident and it took an awful lot of pushing on our part to get that line out of there.
Travelling back and forth from Ottawa to Belleville on the CN, I find that where the CN passenger train travels over the CP track, it is held up by a slow CP freight. I would not say that is done purposely, but it is done frequently. It seems for the sake of three or four minutes that the passenger train could be allowed through rather than made to wait for 30 minutes, as is frequently the case. The co-operation I expect between these two companies, both of which receive support from the federal government, although one to a much greater degree, is much better. Sometimes I am very disappointed.
I want to know whether the railroads will be involved in the planning and whether the CPR, if a plan were developed and approved, would under its legislation be voluntarily asked to co-operate in the disposal of its property. Or would there be legislation forcing the disposal and relocation? If we get that far, how would the lands be disposed of? Would they be left in the hands of the railway to dispose of as they see fit, or be sold or in some way deeded to the municipality to be disposed of as they see fit? Or would there be some different means of disposal? Some of the lands on the shores of the Bay of Quinte are extremely valuable. Others will obviously revert to road allowance and other natural uses.
Perhaps I might have answers to at least some of these questions. I am sure that many of my constituents in the city of Belleville will be most anxious to hear more of this legislation. I share the concern of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. The millions of dollars necessary for such relocation to take place in Belleville would be minuscule in comparison with the cost in the major centres across Canada. None the less, the matter is very important. I want the assurance of the minister that some funds will be made available to us should a decision be made.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the four questions raised by the hon. member, payment for transportation plans and urban development plans is provided for in clause 3(3) on page 3 of the bill. Upon application, the Minister of Transport may pay 50 per cent of the cost of preparing the transportation study or plan and 50 per cent of the preparation of the urban development study or plan. That is the answer to the first question.
With regard to the second question concerning the participation of the railroads, that question was raised by the

previous speaker. There is no way of forcing them to participate, but I certainly think they would. In fact, as one member interjected, the problem would probably be that they would want to take over the whole process.
I would certainly hope that in any relocation planning process the railways would participate. That has certainly been the experience with some smaller relocation schemes. In the studies in Winnipeg-and up until now they have only been studies-the railroads have been extremely active participants in the study and planning process. On the other hand, if people endeavour to exclude them from the planning process, they would have their full rights in front of the CTC to be heard and to put their point of view.
With regard to the third matter of how the land that is freed by relocation is disposed of, this will probably vary from plan to plan. Each city is different and the railway situation in each city is different. It is clearly spelled out in the bill that the plans put before the CTC must spell out specifically how the land is to be disposed of and by whom. It could well be that as part of the plan it is disposed of through the municipality on the private market, or by the railroad. Various combinations and permutations could be developed in any given urban development plan. The plan is subject to hearings and approval by the CTC as well as challenge by those who disagree with the disposal process. It will really depend on each plan.
I make the point, however, that if there is an unwillingness to carry out the disposal plan, the bill provides that the federal Minister of Public Works is given the authority to expropriate the land in order to carry out the urban development plan, which includes the disposal plan. I think in most cases there will be a voluntary arrangement worked out as to what is going to happen. If that is possible, there is power in the legislation to provide for expropriation and disposal.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly on Bill C-27, a bill to facilitate the relocation of railway lines, in order to bring two very precise points to the minister's attention.
First of all, I wish to say that I gladly support this bill, because I feel it is necessary and must be urgently enforced. It is clear, as indicated by the minister and a
April 29, 1974

number of other hon. members, that the railways have contributed to the development of Canadian towns.
In many communities, however, railway lines have become either a source of danger or an impediment to urban development and renewal, especially where railway lines run through center town districts and are a source of a great many problems.
Contrary to what one of my colleages in the Progressive Conservative Party did, I contacted personally the hon. minister some time ago about a legitimate application made by the municipality of Victoriaville which wants to avail itself of the benefits of this bill.
The minister replied quickly and promised to follow up this matter. I want to congratulate him and tell him that I am eager to see the result of the attention he will give to this very important request from the Victoriaville municipality whose development and planning are slowed down by this railway in the centre of town.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw the minister's attention on two matters related to the bill under consideration. If we refer to clause 4 we may read and I quote:
(a) how the costs and benefits of the transportation plan included in the accepted plan are to be shared by the province, the municipalities concerned ...
-and the federal government. So, in paragraph (a) of clause 4, a function is assigned to the province. In clause 8, page 8, a function is assigned to the province as follows:
An order under clause 6 shall be issued only after the Commission is satisfied that the government of the province and each municipality that has agreed to the accepted plan have caused such laws to be passed or such orders to be made as are necessary ...
Therefore there is reference to the necessity to pass that legislation in agreement with the province.
I would like also to quote from the speech of the minister of the House of Commons on April 25, 1974, as recorded on page 1757 of Hansard:
A railway relocation and rerouting project is to begin with provincial and municipal initiatives and calls for participation by all three levels of government.
I want to compliment the minister for acting in co-operation with the three levels of government, but I would express my misgivings concerning the implementation of this legislation. And I wish to remind him of a rather distressing experience that the province of Quebec is undergoing now.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) is aware of what I am talking about, that is famous Bill C-133 that was passed on the National Housing Act. The province of Quebec is one of the provinces that has not benefited as yet from this legislation. Negotiations are still going on. It is not known whether the federal or provincial government is responsible for impeding the implementation of the act, ensuring urban renewal and assisting low income housing construction. Moreover, we all recognize the importance of this legislation in Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to obtain from the minister specific assurances with regards to the method of implementation of the act so that municipalities, big or small, can benefit from it in spite of the little support that could be

given by one province in particular. That application may seem strange to people in other provinces but we in the province of Quebec are faced with this problem, and if the province does not agree or drags a leg the other provinces will benefit from it while we in the province of Quebec wait.
Mr. Chairman, I would find it unfortunate if a province should have a right to veto and refuse it. The minister stated in his speech, and I quote:
... When a province and involved municipalities wish to redevelop a specified urban area,...
-they send an application to Ottawa. Let us suppose a municipality applies to the federal government. What would happen? Is provincial agreement absolutely mandatory? What means do we have available to us to speed up bargaining between the province and the federal government so Quebec municipalities will not be penalized? I do not want to raise a political issue, but strictly an administrative one.
We spend a lot of time in this House passing legislation which I think is good. The one now before us is excellent. But that requires over a year of bargaining between the federal government and the provincial government, and once the bargaining is over municipalities cry for help and the provincial government drags a leg for so-called reasons of autonomy, on the pretext of autonomy.
Mr. Chairman, if I knew that under this act the government of the province of Quebec would have any direct or indirect power of veto I would vote against it because it would be another source of frustration for Quebec municipalities.
I would like to get positive assurance from the minister that he has the true initiative to ensure that municipalities can benefit from that act the implementation of which is absolutely necessary and urgent.
Knowing the interest the minister takes in urban development, urbanization in general and related problems, I am convinced that he understands the kind of question I am now putting to him and that he will provide an adequate answer.

Mr. Speaker, I should just like to say a few words on Bill C-27. Many members have said, as I am sure the minister is well aware, that there has been a patient and pregnant pause between the conception of this measure and its finally reaching the House. We are now considering it in the Committee of the Whole and I realize that there is some disposition to moving it forward. But in my particular area of the country the relocation aspect is not as important as safety features at crossings. This particu-

lar aspect is of very great concern and interest to the people of eastern Canada, and specifically to the people of Nova Scotia and the Annapolis Valley.
On this occasion I should have liked to refer to this matter of priority, as did the hon. member for Red Deer, but perhaps I would be precluded from doing so by the rules. I had in mind a particular reference to an Atlantic transportation policy.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs, who is piloting this bill, made an interesting contribution when the bill first came up for consideration. Representatives from the Atlantic provinces have not been as vocal as we might have been in past years when transportation matters were before the House for consideration, and this is perhaps true particularly in respect of this part of this session and our consideration of certain transportation matters.
The discussion of certain aspects of transportation can be likened almost to the waving of a red flag in front of the proverbial bull. No matter how meritorious and justifiable is this matter of railway relocation and safety at crossings, we from eastern Canada see this as a piecemeal operation in spite of the fact there has been a lot of groundwork. Many of us on this side of the House from eastern Canada recall the great concern about Atlantic transportation expressed during the time when the former minister of transport, the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, brought forward a bill dealing specifically with land transportation and an amendment to the maritime freight rate structure.
We have waited for too long and too patiently for the development and announcement of further policy planks to build that platform which could properly be called an Atlantic transportation policy. While I cannot make a speech about Atlantic transportation policy today under the auspices of this bill, although I would dearly like to, I should like to know what the Minister of Transport and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs have to say about this subject.
While a program to re-route some of our railway lines in cities in Canada may be esthetically desirable, we in the east are more concerned with safety at unmarked crossings, or at crossings that are marked but inadequately so. I have not been able to find any reference to a schedule of costs applicable to the railway companies in respect of relocation. I have not found any specific reference to the proposed disposition of what might be called special purpose buildings located on railway property in various areas across Canada.
In this regard I have particular reference to water towers, water tanks or even old roundhouses which were constructed to serve specific purposes. Ordinarily under our laws of expropriation the railways are justified in requesting a replacement value for those special purpose buildings, even though the railway companies as well as municipal and provincial authorities know that these buildings are redundant and that the railways should not be allowed to follow the normal expropriation proceedings in asking for full replacement value. As a result of technological advances these buildings and facilities have become redundant.
