subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL CAMPAIGN TO PROMOTE HIGHWAY SAFETY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should immediately initiate, in co-operation with provincial governments and appropriate organizations, a national campaign to promote driving safety throughout Canada in the interests of preservation of human life and courtesy among the driving public.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to propose this motion, I wish first to deal with a fundamental question that will trouble at least some hon. members. At the outset I wish to state that this motion is presented with deep seriousness and strong conviction. In this milieu we are often tempted to approach the actions of other members with scepticism bordering on cynicism. Perhaps this is an unavoidable aspect of partisan policies, but it is unfortunate and I hope will not taint consideration of a motion that I can solemnly assure hon. members is not presented as a so-called "motherhood" issue.
Along these lines perhaps I might be permitted to give the background to this resolution. It is customary, Mr. Speaker, for a private member to use his one motion per session to advance a personally felt cause, often based on a particular need of his constituency. Last session, in keeping with that practice, I used my motion to call upon the government to conduct a full inquiry into its plans for an expanded Hamilton civic airport. Although the motion, again in keeping with custom, did not come to a vote, I was indeed pleased when the government finally acted and implemented that suggestion.
Accordingly, it might have well been anticipated that my motion for this session would deal with an issue of special concern to Hamilton-Wentworth, such as the failure of this government to deal adequately with the high water levels on the Great Lakes. Instead, I have chosen to

April 29, 1974
Road Safety
deal with a most grievous situation which affects my constituency as it does all others, and one which should be of special interest to none less than every member of this House.
Last August, The Spectator, the daily newspaper of the Hamilton area, contacted local politicians, including myself, to obtain their reaction to the appalling increase in traffic fatalities and to ask what these elected officials could or would do about the situation. The report on this survey reads as follows:
Local politicians expressed shock and horror over the people killed on area roads so far this year. And a number pledged action on the ever-mounting massacre.
I was quoted later in that same report as saying:
One can't be oblivious or complacent about these statistics-
-referring to the traffic death totals, and I went on to say:
The fact that there needs to be many things done is a demand upon every member of parliament.
My feelings about our common responsibility have only grown in their intensity as I have examined this issue further, and that is why I have chosen this opportunity to fulfil, in some measure, the commitment made those many months ago. That is why I am inviting this House to join me in urging the federal government to initiate a coordinated program with the provinces to promote highway safety and driving courtesy throughout Canada.
This, in turn, raises the question as to the efficacy of such programs. These have recently been brought into question as the result of a recent story in an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on April 19 of this year. But just this morning, in that same newspaper, Dr. G. J. S. Wilde, a professor of psychology at Queen's University at Kingston, dealt with the question of the efficiency and efficacy of safety minded programs. He said:
A road safety campaign is not necessarily a waste of money if one considers the benefits during the time before the effects wear off. Several examples of cost-effective campaigns are known to professionals who work in the field of road accident prevention. The savings in medical expenses alone outweigh the publicity costs of campaigns such as The Green Cross Code and the Newcastle seat belt campaign in the United Kingdom. In addition, major reductions in human suffering were achieved.
Closer to home, the campaign directed against drinking and driving in Edmonton in 1972 significantly reduced blood alcohol levels in drivers. Sweden saved 20 per cent of its road deaths immediately following the changeover from left-hand to right-hand traffic, and road fatalities in Britain were reduced by more than 1,000 after their law of .08 blood alcohol came into effect.
Thus, short-term effects may be "onsiderable even if they do not last.
More important to bear in mind is that at stake are the lives of Canadians, both those foolhardy enough to endanger their own lives and the lives of their all-too-frequent innocent victims. The Canada Safety Council, in a report giving the latest available figures, which covers the year 1972 and which was sent to every hon. member, provides us with disturbing data that indicate the gravity of the situation.
Of the 12,825 total accidental fatalities, the leading cause, by far, was motor vehicle accidents, which accounted for 48.6 per cent of the total. The motor vehicle fatality rate increased from 26 per cent per 100,000 population in the previous year to 28.6 per cent.

In less statistical and perhaps more real terms, 6,237 men, women and children died in 1972 from motor vehicle accidents. And while the data is not yet fully compiled, the numbers, the deaths, keep rising.
Most distressing of all is the grim picture of 771 young Canadians under age 15, looking forward to a full life in a nation that could offer them so much, a nation desirous and deserving of their unique contributions, dying, together with their dreams and their promise, in that same year. Of all accidental deaths involving young people in 1972, 43 per cent were attributable to traffic tragedies, thus reflecting a continuing trend.
We cannot bring back those victims, but neither can we justify those murders. We who remain can do a service to those victims by recalling their passing with a horror that compels each of us to do everything within our personal and collective power to avoid the future loss of lives in such an inglorious and unnecessary cause as the automobile.
My resolution does not pretend to be an ultimate solution. Nor does it attempt to suggest that the federal government has been derelict in its responsibility. I have no doubt that spokesmen for the government will rise in this debate to proclaim the efforts of the federal government to promote traffic safety. In anticipation of those comments I do acknowledge and commend those responsible for safety minded programs such as the promotion of child safety week during the first week of May.
If this chamber had representatives of our provincial governments and the various safety agencies, we could also expect them to rise and rhyme off their individual contributions to driving safety. Again these activities are worthy of commendation.
But my point is that all these governments, agencies and their respective programs would have greater effect and greater chances of success if their efforts were better co-ordinated. A national conference to share the experiences of their individual programs could benefit all participants in their common goal of traffic safety and driving courtesy. I mention driving courtesy in my motion because I believe it to be the very basis of safe driving. The machines and roads we use are meant for living, not for dying, when used properly and in accordance with the laws experience has helped to develop. It is concern for others that prompts driving courtesy and which in turn makes the roads safe.
It is my fervent hope and belief that a great common effort would be more effective and would be justified if its outcome were the saving of even one innocent life from yet another traffic calamity. And so, Mr. Speaker, I present a motion that is non-partisan and constructive the federal government. It might truly be said that this motion is deadly serious in its intent. I hope that the House will consider and endorse this motion in the same spirit with which it is presented.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL CAMPAIGN TO PROMOTE HIGHWAY SAFETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member no doubt proposed this motion in the express hope that a nationwide effort to combat the road safety problem
April 29, 1974

would lead to a lessening in the number of casualties suffered on our roads each year. I wholeheartedly support this basic intent, as I am sure do all Canadians, particularly in face of the mounting toll of road casualties now exceeding 6,000 persons killed and 200,000 persons injured each year.
The motion as proposed recommends "a national campaign to promote driving safety." There is a certain ambiguity in the use of the term "campaign". It may, for example, simply imply a propaganda or public education campaign. Or the term may be used in its broader sense implying an integrated program.
If we are to interpret "campaign" in the narrow sense of a propaganda campaign, then I submit that this in itself is not the best approach to take in combatting the road safety problem. Road safety campaigns can be very expensive to develop and run. And they can, with distressing frequency, be totally ineffective in meeting their objective of reducing road casualties, as witness an American campaign sponsored by the National Safety Council to increase seat belt usage levels. This campaign cost over $50 million, and had no measurable effect on the proportion of vehicle occupants wearing seat belts.
An international group of experts in public education reported in 1971 that "many safety campaigns of the last decade or so simply could not have the desired effect because they were not planned in accordance with what is presently known about behavior modification through mass communication." The group, which met under the auspices of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, reviewed the effectiveness of many public education campaigns and concluded that such campaigns are more likely to be effective when co-ordinated with other road safety programs, such as legislation and enforcement.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, despite the best of motivations on the part of the developers of public education campaigns, and in spite of the most lavish of expenditures, we cannot expect that public education will be effective just as a matter of course. We must not panic and, like the proverbial headless chicken, scurry around demanding that somebody do something, regardless of its ultimate worth, just so that we get some action.
On the other hand, if the hon. member's intention was to recommend an attack on road accidents on all fronts, then he is on the right track and I would agree with him. I can assure the hon. member that the government is greatly concerned over the road safety problem and considers the development and implementation of proven counter measures to be a top priority.
In February of this year federal and provincial cabinet ministers responsible for road safety and motor vehicle administration announced their intention to increase cooperation in the form of a co-ordinated five year program to improve highway safety in Canada. In a press release on February 22 it was stated that the goal of this program is to reduce the nation's road traffic fatality rate by 15 per cent over the next five years.
Senior officials from the 11 governments met in Ottawa in March to discuss Canada's road safety programs in the light of this goal. As expressed in a joint statement on
Road Safety
March 29 at the conclusion of their discussions, agreement was reached that the greatest potential for reduction in the fatality rate lies in:
1.	Increasing the use of seat belts.
2.	Reducing the extent of driving while impaired by alcohol through changes in the Criminal Code and increased public education.
3.	Identification and correction of hazardous road locations.
4.	Emphasis on improving the safety of trucks, buses and school buses through the motor vehicle safety standards program.
5.	Improved vehicle maintenance particularly for commercial vehicles through public information and improved service of vehicle inspection.
6.	Extension and improvement of driver education programs.
7.	Increased police presence.
It was the opinion of these officials that progress must be made in these areas if we are to meet the road safety goal of a 15 per cent reduction in Canada's road traffic fatality rate over the next five years. Despite major efforts to date in safety regulations, road improvement and vehicle design, further action by all levels of government, safety organizations and individual drivers is necessary if the annual escalation of road casualties is to be reversed.
The House will note that public education was mentioned in a number of contexts in the program areas recommended at the federal-provincial meeting. There is no doubt that public education will play a very significant role in the co-operative road safety program that will be implemented over the next five years.
Allow me to elaborate further on those road safety counter measures which offer the greatest likelihood of improvement in our road fatality rate. First of all, there is the question of seat belt usage. There is no doubt in my mind that increasing seat belt usage would be the single and most effective advance that could be made at this time. Seat belts have been required to be installed in all seating positions of new motor vehicles since 1971 in Canada. In practice most automotive vehicles have been equipped with belts since 1966 or even earlier. However, belt usage rates are disappointingly low.
The problem of increasing usage rates has most frequently been tackled by mass media campaigns exhorting people to "buckle up," or asking "Are you putting me on?" This type of public education campaign has been largely ineffective. Public education is more likely to change the public's awareness of the value of seat belts and to make them more receptive to other counter measures that may be introduced, such as ignition interlock systems or possibly seat belt use legislation.
The second area recommended for high priority attention by the federal and provincial road safety officials is the alcohol impaired driving problem. The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1969 made it an offence for a driver of a motor vehicle to have a blood alcohol content in excess of .08 per cent. The same amendment made it compulsory for a driver to submit to a breath test, when the request to do so is made by a police officer on reasonable grounds.

April 29, 1974
Road Safety
The federal Department of Transport conducted an expensive public education campaign at that time to inform the public of the amendment and its provisions. Before and after telephone surveys evaluated the effectiveness of this campaign. The results were impressive. The public's knowledge of all the amendment's provisions increased substantially. For example, whereas in the before study only 12 per cent of persons responding were aware that the legal limit was .08 per cent, in the after group 72 per cent of the people could quote this figure.
As effective as this campaign was in informing the public, it should not be assumed that a change in knowledge on the part of the driving public will necessarily result in a change in behavior. A recent study released by the Department of Transport indicates that the so-called breathalizer legislation was largely ineffective in reducing the involvement of alcohol in serious accidents. So while the campaign succeeded in imparting knowledge, it did not succeed, in conjunction with changes in legislation and enforcement methods, in producing the desired behavioral change, namely a reduction in the amount of alcohol-impaired driving in Canada.
The impaired driving problem will not be easily resolved. However, it will retain its position as a priority research and program area because of the seriousness of the problem. It has been demonstrated in numerous excellent studies that alcohol is a factor in fully 50 per cent of all fatal road accidents on this continent.
The road safety officials also recognized the role played by the road network itself in contributing to the occurrence and severity of road accidents. Most highway departments have ongoing programs to identify and treat hazardous road locations. Whether the hazard be a roadside obstacle, a geometric design feature of the roadway-I mean the dangerous curve or hill-or a maintenance hazard dealing with ice or snow, of prime importance to the highway department is the accurate identification of the location and its hazardous features. Once the problem has been identified, the most appropriate remedial action can then be taken to alleviate the hazard.
Of major importance is the effect of hazards on the roadside on the severity of accidents. Eighteen per cent of all road accidents in Canada during 1972 involved single vehicles which ran off the road and rolled or struck an obstacle. However, 27 per cent of all fatal accidents were of this type.
Specifically, a list of counter measures proven effective includes the removal of unnecessary roadside fixed objects, the protection of necessary fixed objects with energy attenuation devices such as collapsible barriers at gore areas, improved guardrail design, and the replacement of structures with solid bases by those with breakaway or frangible bases.
Of course, these are expensive solutions, so it will be necessary to establish priorities and to correct those hazardous road locations that will return the most benefit per dollar expended. The Department of Transport is presently engaged in a research project specifically designed to establish procedures for developing these priorities. A

number of provinces have already committed major sums of money for the removal of road hazards.
I am told that consideration was also given at the meeting to priority areas involving the vehicles that use the road system. A specific concern was expressed for the safety of commercial vehicles, including trucks, buses and school buses. More rigid safety standards can be expected for these vehicles through the motor vehicle safety standards program. The safety standards deal with motor vehicles at the time of their manufacture. The extent to which these vehicles retain their safety characteristics depends to a great degree on how they are maintained. The provincial officials reported their considerable interest in improving the level of vehicle maintenance-particularly for commercial vehicles-through augmented public information and vehicle inspection programs.
It should be noted that the federal government has responsibility for but a portion of these priority road safety program areas. The provinces and municipalities have major areas of responsibility in road safety, such as driver licensing, training and police enforcement, as well as those mentioned previously. Therefore it is heartening to see the importance placed at all levels of government on co-ordination of effort in areas of both safety research, program development and program implementation. The provincial and federal governments are committed to documenting their existing road programs with an eye to improving the exchange of program information between government levels and among many countries on an international basis. More attention will be put on program evaluation in the future, with the intention of continually refining and developing those program areas that show themselves most effective.
I think we must face the fact that the road safety problem is not an easy one to solve. There are no simplistic solutions; there are no royal roads to safe driving. Through the "fifties and" sixties progress has been made in improving the road and the vehicle. The continually increasing demand for vehicular transportation in this country, as in all the world, will continue to make it exceedingly difficult to make absolute reductions in the number of road casualties. However, the government believes that it will only be through an integrated and well-developed road safety program, with major effort from government, industry and the general populace, that possible improvements can be realized.
I am advised, Mr. Speaker, that it is precisely this approach that the government is taking.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL CAMPAIGN TO PROMOTE HIGHWAY SAFETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address a few remarks to the motion of the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan), I do so with a deep appreciation for the importance of driver safety counter measures. I share the concern of all members of the House, I am sure, when it comes to the problem of traffic safety. I rise to speak today with the confident knowledge that Canada, and the government in particular, has not been remiss in its duty to deal positively with the problem of traffic deaths and injuries.
As my hon. colleague has just mentioned, the representatives participating in the recent federal-provincial
April 29, 1974

meeting on road safety identified a number of areas for concentration. One of the areas singled out for special attention was the need for reducing the extent of driving while impaired by alcohol. I wish to discuss this problem today in light of the hon. member's motion for a national road safety campaign.
The effects of alcohol in traffic accidents have been well documented and there can be no doubt left in anyone's mind as to the seriousness of this problem. It is estimated that in Canada 50 per cent of all driver fatalities can be linked to the effects of alcohol. Of these, roughly 80 per cent have a blood alcohol content of .10 per cent or greater, even though the law in Canada states that it is illegal to operate a motor vehicle if the blood alcohol content is .08 per cent or more.
Before I describe a few of the steps that have been taken to find solutions to the drinking and driving problem, I would first like to ask, "Who is the drinking driver"? As a recent Department of Transport report on alcohol and highway safety points out,
There is strong evidence from existing studies, that whiie the problem drinkers and alcoholics make up a small proportion of the total population, they account for a very considerable part of the over-all problem of traffic fatalities.
The results of past studies on criminological, sociological and psychological factors relating to drinking drivers have revealed a character analysis of the drinking driver as predominantly male, and if I may quote further:
The highest levels of blood alcohol are frequently found, not in the very young, nor in the older drivers, but in persons between the mid-twenties to the mid-fifties. Those drivers who are divorced, separated, or have relatively low levels of education, are also more likely to drive after drinking. Personality studies of individuals apprehended for driving after heavy drinking have pointed at the high incidence of paranoid ideation, self-destructiveness, suicidal tendencies, hostility, obsessional rumination, manual occupation, criminal records, neuroti-cism, extraversion, social immaturity and willingness to accept risks.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to reach these individuals by mass publicity or any other device presently available for use.
The government is continuing research into the study of types of drinking drivers and it is hoped that the results will enable more effective programs to be designed. The drinking and driving problem has been approached in two ways. The first is in the legal area of strict laws and enforcement. The second is an extensive national and international research program.
The .08 per cent or breathalyzer section of the Criminal Law Amendment Act became law in December, 1969. The effects of this counter measure have been monitored to determine the results. It was anticipated that we would find a reduction in fatal accidents. A recent Department of Transport survey indicates that a small reduction in fatalities was realized the first year, 1970, but unfortunately the law is no longer effecting a decrease. In the light of the situation it is clear that we must continue to search for more effective methods. The representatives at the federal-provincial meeting agreed that changes in the legislation, together with a major education campaign to gain support from the public, might be an effective means of overcoming this problem.
In saying this, I do not wish to imply that the law enforcement officials have been lax in their duty, for we
Road Safety
all know the tremendous and difficult task they face in identifying the drunk drivers. Because a person is charged with a criminal offence when his blood alcohol content is over .08, per cent law enforcement officials have to be extremely cautious before they submit someone to a breath test. Consequently, the average readings across Canada for those persons being charged is .16 per cent, double the legal level of impairment.
What I would like to suggest is that the police need help in more accurately identifying the offenders. To this end research on roadside screening methods is continuing, and hopefully it will have two worthwhile outcomes. The first is to assure that a suspected drinking driver is not unnecessarily inconvenienced and, secondly, to assure that those at the lower levels of impairment are not escaping detection.
Canada had responsibility for the alcohol and highway safety sub-project of the NATO Pilot Study in Road Safety and has completed a report which reviews the alcohol/driving countermeasures that have been tried in many countries and suggests which ones warrant further examination. It is clear that there is no one solution to this problem and that much more information is needed about the extent of drinking/driving before valid comparisons of countermeasure effectiveness can be made. The study therefore recommends that roadside surveys, designed to obtain a measure of blood alcohol in drivers, be conducted in all member countries. A protocol for conducting these roadside surveys was developed and is included as a part of the final report.
Roadside surveys have been used in Canada to evaluate the effectiveness of drinking and driving campaigns as well as to gather information of the blood alcohol content of drivers on the roads during the day and evening hours.
In 1971, for example, a roadside survey in Alberta was conducted in conjunction with a public education campaign to discourage drinking and driving over the Christmas season. This was a joint effort between the federal Ministry of Transport and the Canada Safety Council. The measure of success obtained indicates that this method of public education campaign may be a potentially effective means of lowering the incidence of drunk-driving over the critical Christmas season.
So far I have confined my remarks to the Canadian government's national and international activities, but let us not forget the dedicated involvement of each of the provincial governments in designing provincial programs, or the Canada Safety Council, the Traffic Injury Research Foundation or the various other safety-minded groups too numerous to mention who have worked dedicatedly across Canada to increase Canada's awareness of the problem and to encourage us all to make a concentrated effort to lower traffic accident statistics.
Although, Mr. Speaker, I have restricted my comments to the problem of drinking and driving I am well aware that this is but one element of the federal-provincial co-operative program already referred to by my hon. colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, although I shall speak for only a moment or two, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan) on using his one and only private member's motion during this session to raise the important subject of driving safety. I commend him for the forceful speech he made and hope that by the time he has been here for as long as some of the rest of us, the picture regarding deaths on our highways will have altered greatly.
I suppose one could predict, as the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth did, that spokesmen on the government side would give us a list of all the things the government has done in trying to cope with motor vehicle carnage; yet I enjoin my good friend from Hamilton-Wentworth not to be cynical about it. I say that because the list of things mentioned by spokesmen on the other side underlines that there are many factors which contribute to automobile accidents and to the loss of life. It is good to know that there is concern about all these important causes and problems.
Both of the members on the government side who have spoken thus far said a good deal about the part alcohol plays in automobile accidents. Certainly, the statistics tell a gruesome story in that respect. There was reference to the efforts to lay down standards for the manufacture of cars, so that they will be built with safety features. There was reference to making more universal the use of seat belts, to extensive driver training and driver licensing programs, and there have also been comments on the need for intelligent and effective engineering of our highways. A great deal has been done in this area in recent decades in terms of making highways more safe, getting rid of obstacles to vision and getting rid of those things which increase the number of accidents.
I hope mv friend from Hamilton-Wentworth joins me in welcoming the list of things to which attention has been paid. We also make the point that the incidence of deaths which take place because of automobile accidents is so high, so serious, that we need to double and redouble our efforts to prevent accidents. The extent of loss of life because of motor vehicle accidents is one of the most gruesome scandals of the twentieth century. When one considers the number of human beings who have lost their lives in motor vehicle accidents since 1900, one wonders whether the human race is as sensible as it claims to be.
Regardless of what happens to the present motion raised in today's private members' hour, the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth has done a service by raising the issue. I join with him in calling for doubled and redoubled effort in all ways that can cut down the loss of life on our highways. I say to the hon. member that he has done well to raise this issue. I call on him to stick with it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak about the bill before us as I consider it is a matter of general interest. I entirely agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that it is our duty, not only as members of Parliament but also as Canadian citizens, to strive harder than ever to reduce the mortality rate on Canadian highways. I wish to commend the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan) who in

his bill, gives hon. members an opportunity to discuss during this hour the problem facing us.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, even if I entirely agree with the motion, I have some reservations because I do not think that the general education programs and the publicity made through television, radio and so on will change the attitude of Canadian citizens about highways and the way they are used.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I think it is essential that we teach the youth at the primary or secondary education level and pursuade them to take the necessary precautions for using the transportation system at our disposal.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, everyone knows that it is at this level that preventive action is most efficient. In fact, it is at the age when children are rather impressionable that we must direct our efforts. I entirely agree that it might be profitable for publicity agencies to receive contracts from provincial and federal governments to communicate information concerning road safety but nevertheless it is in the present educational system and within the existing framework that we should concentrate more and more our efforts.
There is another problem with regard to the instruments we have for transportation purposes. We have our roads and our automobiles. I come from an area that is discriminated against in so far as road safety is concerned. Indeed, in my area of northern Ontario, the roads are horrible. Most accidents are not caused by driver neglect, but the condition of the roads.
Highway 64 which runs from the southern to the northern portion of the province connects with highways 17 and 11.1 am sure I am accurate when I state that road has been responsible for more deaths in the past generation than any other stretch of road in Canada. The portion between Sturgeon Falls and Field is one of the worst pieces of pavement ever constructed and maintained by man. I admit that road comes within provincial jurisdiction, but in his motion the hon. member recognizes that the provincial government has to be involved in this particular program. Numerous representations have been made to the Ontario government, but they have refused so far to improve that road. They have refused to consider the essential nature of transportation in northern Ontario and the necessity of maintaining highways in good condition.
Although this did not relate to road safety, I might indicate that during the months of March and April the only industry in the town of Field, Field Lumber, was closed because of the half-load limit imposed by the Ontario government on that road. They will impose a half-load limit, but refuse to improve the condition of that road to make it useable by industry and private citizens.
There is also considerable difficulty as a result of automobile design. This, too, results in discrimination with regard to road safety in Canada. Indeed, the fact that automobiles used in Canada are designed in the United States is detrimental to road safety. There is no doubt that American cars, which are used predominantly in Canada, are great for the toll roads and main highways in the
April 29, 1974

United States, but they do not do the job when transplanted to northern Ontario.
I have a Pontiac Ventura. I find it necessary to carry about 250 pounds of bricks and concrete blocks in the trunk in order to maintain the stability of that car on icy roads in northern Ontario. I might also point out that when driving in the snow in northern Ontario, the ventilation system sucks the snow that is flying around into the cab, completely fogging the inside of the windshield. If these are not errors in design of major proportions, I do not know what to call them. Accepting American design without question contributes more to danger than any other factor. Because of unsafe roads such as highway 64, and the design and engineering of automobiles, residents of northern Ontario are further discriminated against.
I am sure that the automobile insurance rates are higher in my area of northern Ontario than anywhere else in the province. I do not relate that to the quality of driving. Surely, drivers in northern Ontario are as qualified as those in southern Ontario. I relate this directly to the unsatisfactory conditions of the roads in northern Ontario and the unsatisfactory design of the automobiles that ply them. I suggest that greater attention be given to those two faults.

Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that we would all like to live in a country where going from one place to another poses no problems. I know that courtesy on the road leaves much to be desired. It is imperative that Canadian drivers acquire better habits. We must also consider as essential the implementation of an information program to better educate the public and instil in it a greater respect for our driving laws and human life.
Mr. Speaker, in our area, few families have been spared the tragedy of a fatal accident on the road. Those tragedies must of all necessity be avoided. At one time, we thought that by imposing limits to the level of inebriation tolerated on the road we would reduce somewhat the number of fatal accidents. There was considerable publicity about the measures the police would take to prevent people from using the road and their car when intoxicated or almost. Unfortunately, in spite of the relevant publicity, we notice that proceedings, because of the breathalizer test, did not have the expected effect. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that this is so, but I am coming back to my first remarks saying that it would not be through legal sanctions that you will stop people from abusing the transportation system. Neither will it be through a system of general education applied through a means of information that the situation will be changed. You must first return to the young and educate them within the prevalent educational system. We should ask the governments of Ontario and of the other provinces, and the federal government, to save some funds for this purpose.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, in a nationalist context such as ours, we must also prepare cars for our Canadian climate to carry us from point A to point B in total security. Mr. Speaker, I would like to invite the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth to encourage his fellow members of the provincial party to take measures to improve roads, the pavement so that we in northern Ontario could enjoy road safety. All citizens of Ontario
Road Safety
should benefit from cars equipped for winter, cars which can stand two winters and, furthermore, should have insurance rates comparable to southern Ontario. This comes under provincial jurisdiction; however, Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth for giving me the chance to show the provincial governments that it is necessary to improve road conditions. It is also a provincial responsibility to see that cars come under road security standards.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL CAMPAIGN TO PROMOTE HIGHWAY SAFETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate on the motion of the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan). Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I wish to congratulate him for giving us this opportunity to discuss a serious matter, one which affects the safety of so many of our citizens. Members in all quarters of the House are much concerned about the numbers of people who are killed or injured every year on our highways and we are all in accord, I think, in our views on this important issue.
We have at hand the single, most effective weapon for combatting the tragic loss of life on our nation's highways. I am referring, of course, to seat belts. The evidence is unanimous that seat belts work, that they are effective in reducing deaths and injuries resulting from traffic accidents. Recent Canadian research on seat belts gave rise to the following conclusion:
The studies which were reviewed generally agree that with total usage of lap and shoulder belts, fatalities could be reduced by half. This means that in Canada, in 1972, more than 1,700 vehicle occupant fatalities would have been saved if everyone had been wearing the seat belts available.
No similar claim can be made with regard to any other immediately available counter measure. There is no other readily available measure to reduce the toll of death and injury from traffic accidents which could approach the potential to be realized by the universal use of seat belts.
In fact, the Canadian government, through the Motor Vehicles Safety Act and regulations, has recognized the importance of seat belts by requiring their fitment in all new automobiles sold in Canada after January 1, 1971. These regulations are continually being up-dated to take account of new technology. The latest change, effective January 1, 1974, required fitment of the best currently available seat belt design, the three-point lap and shoulder combination with inertia-reel, a truly comfortable and easy-to-use system.
Current seat belt research is aimed toward developing "passive" seat belts. Such a belt deploys automatically about the occupant as he seats himself in his vehicle and stows itself automatically as he leaves the vehicle. In its other aspects it is similar to the belts currently being installed in new vehicles. Prototype models indicate that these belts retain all the advantages of the conventional belt yet dispense with the requirement for any action on the part of the driver or passenger, at a relatively low cost. This system holds great potential and it is my view that its
27451-54i

April 29, 1974
Relocation of Railway Lines
development should be hastened, perhaps by government action.
Even though it is indisputable that the wearing of seat belts reduces the risk of death and injury, and even though seat belts are available today in the vast majority of cars, the percentage who actually wear these devices is still very low-probably no more than 10 per cent or 15 per cent of vehicle occupants. Fully aware of this, the government has sought to influence usage by direct, legislative means. Since July 1, 1972, legislation has required that automobiles be equipped with a buzzer-light warning system which activates if seat belts are not fastened while the car is operating. However, due to the relative ease with which these devices can be by-passed, they have not proved particularly successful in promoting usage.
Public education campaigns have long been regarded by governments as a method by which the wearing of seat belts is encouraged. Unfortunately, most of them have been based on an incomplete understanding of the processes at work, and, hence, have failed. In the words of the review of seat belt usage habits in 16 European countries:
The information and education campaigns so far conducted have been largely successful in convincing drivers and passengers of the usefulness of seat belts, but have had limited effect in inducing vehicle occupants to actually wear them, doubtless because insufficiently strong motivation exists.
Governments have available to them a method for providing this motivation. Laws prescribing that seat belts shall be worn have proven effective in several countries, notably in Australia. The director of the New South Wales traffic accident research unit said in July, 1972:
Surveys of seat belt wearing ... showed that the percentage of those wearing seat belts in front seat positions rose from around 25 per cent before legislation to around 75 per cent very soon afterward.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know there are other members who want to speak on this as well as other clauses of this bill, so at this stage I will keep my remarks short. Clause 3 under Part I, respecting joint urban development and transportation plans, begins to outline a litte more fully the objectives of this bill in respect of relocation of rails in certain urban areas of the country, along with the development of more safety features at railways crossings. I understand that this plan also applies in respect of rural areas.
Before we recessed for dinner, I had referred to transportation in this country as being somewhat symptomatic of the lack of transportation policy in this country. I appreciate that this is perhaps not the time to make a comprehensive speech on transportation matters throughout the country, and specifically in Atlantic Canada, but I should point out in passing that the Minister of Transport confessed not long ago that transportation was in a mess.
After 11 years under this present government, perhaps the Minister of Transport is to be complimented for his frankness as exemplified by his confession that transportation generally, and specifically in respect of policy, was in an absolute mess in this country. I do not think he used the word, "absolute", but he certainly said it was in a mess. As we sit on this side of the House considering different piecemeal approaches under different ministers of transport to this whole matter of transportation, we can only echo that transportation is in a bad way across the country. Whether this particular bill should be supported by all members of this House because it will help unify safety features in respect of railway crossings in various cities is a matter for debate, nevertheless this bill does not offer any solutions for the fundamental problems of transportation.
This country was born, grew and developed on the basis of its transportation, and whether we are free enterprise socialists, liberal socialists, as we call them today, or Conservatives we must all agree that it was the CPR, the link between the east and the west, that finally drew this country together. Ironically, in this day of communications and increased technology, it is perhaps the problems of transportation or the lack of a transportation policy in the national sense that is really causing some of the divisiveness and disunity in this country. But here we have Bill C-27 which will make more beautiful some of our urban areas in Canada, which will perhaps take down some water tanks, shift some roundhouses and engage in other like ventures as well as perhaps help to improve safety on the road and relocate railway crossings across the country.
The Minister of Transport who is not in the House right now, confessed that Canada has no transportation policy. I
April 29, 1974

wonder what was the reason for this confession. I was a member of this House, as were other members on this side and some on the opposite side, when that great bill on the national transportation policy was brought to the House. It was supposed to revolutionize the concept of transportation in this country. All modes of transport were supposed to charge what the traffic would bear. As a result of that bill the Canadian Transport Commission was established headed by the former minister of transport, Mr. Pickers-gill, at a very interesting and rewarding salary. Then, we went from the Pickersgillian pork barrel to the late minister of finance-I say "late" although he is still very much with us but is no longer minister of finance here-who became the next chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission.
I wonder if perhaps one of the problems of transportation-be it railway crossings or relocation of railway crossings in the centre of the city-is that politics, political appointments and political necessities have been the dominant considerations governing many of the decisions of this government. Regardless of the personalities of the chairmen of the CTC, whether it was Mr. Pickersgill, Mr. Benson or whoever else may become the next chairman, this is not the way to decide the transportation policy and the future of our railways.
Speaking of railways, there is something that has not received much attention since the recent appointments. We have two national railroads, the CPR and the CNR, and here again one wonders if perhaps politics are not influencing the decisions that are being made in the running of these two corporations. We have a brand new president and a brand new chairman of the CNR. The former president, Mr. MacMillan, was evidently doing a good job so that he has had to be replaced by two individuals. One would have thought that this government might have learned from the experience of Air Canada that when you diminish the responsibility of a chief executive, and this is especially true in transportation-on when you start to divide that responsibility, you find that the organization does not have the drive that it would have had under one chief executive officer. Personally, I do not know the two new gentlemen who are running the CNR, but judging from the experience of Air Canada and the fact that two individuals were appointed by this government to run that corporation, this mistake should not have been made again because Air Canada has run into a lot of problems.
If we really wanted to look into the problems of Air Canada tonight, I would have to go into greater detail to outline them than I am permitted under this bill. But here we are doing the same thing with the CNR. I do not know the background of these two gentlemen who are now replacing the president of the CNR and I do not know whether they were formerly CNR vice-presidents, but I do know that one of them has not been very long with the railway. However, I wonder whether that is the way to solve some of the problems of the CNR. So, here we have the Canadian Transport Commission, which is one of the main bodies responsible for implementing the policy under this bill, and the CNR, which is one of the two main railways affected by this bill. We will put a postage stamp here, do a patchwork job there, but in terms of a fundamental transportation policy we are not facing the reali-
Relocation of Railway Lines
ties and putting forward solutions that some of these pressing problems deserve.
I am sorry to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare leave the House, but may I suggest that with his great experience in piloting the football legislation through the House, and having been the grey eminence behind the throne before he was elected, he might have been useful in curing some of the sicknesses in the transportation system of this country. Perhaps instead of concentrating on football and worrying about health and welfare, if we are really going to carry this dual concept to an extreme-the Russians wanted a troika at the head of the United Nations so that no one could do anything but we prefer dual authority in the CNR and Air Canada- perhaps we could have the minister move out of his legislative role and help Mr. Benson. Perhaps, we should have him move into the CTC to help balance the Benson rudder with a Lalonde rudder.

speechtext: Perhaps we could do the same with the Minister of Supply and Services.

speechtext:
No, I would not want him to go anywhere.
I know that there are other hon. members who want to speak on this bill. I do not have anything critical to say of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs who is piloting this bill. This is basically a transport bill, a transport problem. Although it affects cities it also affects many rural parts of Canada. I know that the Minister of Transport, who has a lot of intestinal fortitude, is not hiding behind the skirts or the suit of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, but when you have the Minister of Transport in a government that has been in power in this country for 11 years con-fesssing that our transportation policy is a mess and that the only thing we can do is to adopt a bandaid approach to certain localized problems, then I say it is time something was done. The eastern part of Canada is dependent on a viable transportation policy, something we were promised in 1969 by the then minister of transport.
Our problem is centred around the maritime freight rates policy. I say that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion will have real problems on his hands with regard to that. I am glad to see him come into the House- there must be some telepathy between us. If the maritime freight rates subsidy, which is as basic to Eastern transportation as are the Crowsnest pass rates to the west, is affected then the shipment of goods from one part of the country to another will also be affected so that viable industry will be hard pressed to continue, let alone to expand, on the basis of this type of policy. I say that this government has grave problems, and yet here we are talking about railway relocation and the safety of railway crossings.
I know that there are other hon. members who want to say a few more words on this bill. All I have to say about railway safety and railway relocation is that the sooner we come to grips with the fundamental problems in the country, the better off we will be. The most fundamental problem right now is to find out where the government of this country is and who is running this country so that we can have a government making decisions on basic questions in all areas, not just on transportation policy. Canadians will really only have real safety when they

relocate this government on the opposition side and have this party go to the government side. Then a policy will be adopted affecting railway crossings, affecting urban beauty and improvement, but fundamentally creating a viable transportation system and making this a better country for all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, thank you for recognizing me. I would like to speak about clause 3 of Bill C-27.
Before the dinner hour, I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) to give me a guarantee or a concrete assurance about the bill we are studying and I hope we will pass it so that it will apply from one ocean to the other, and make all Canadians equal under the law, in spite of often hardly inexplicable wills in certain provinces.
The minister did not well understand what I said, i.e. what would happen if a municipality located in another province wanted to benefit from the bill under study. Could it do it? The minister answered that this was against the principle of consultation with or intervention by the provinces.
But this was not the question. I was only repeating what Hansard said he said on page 1757.
The House is now studying clause 3. I would like to be very exact about this. It is said and I quote:
3. (1) Where, in respect of an area in a province that includes or comprises an urban area ... the government of the province and all the municipalities within that area have agreed upon an urban development plan and transportation plan (hereinafter in this Part called an "accepted plan") ...
-up to then, all goes well, there are no problems. I continue quoting clause 3:
... for that transportation study area, the province or a municipality...
-this is what the minister told me before lunch. In answer to my question, he referred to clause 3 where it is stipulated that "the province or a municipality-"
But the minister did not then continue the quotation. But, if you continue, you can see on line 10-
... the province or a municipality acting on behalf of the province .. .
Which means, Mr. Chairman, that a province, no matter what its needs, its situation or the common interests of the people living in this urban area, will not be able to avail itself of the benefits of this bill which, I hope, will be endorsed by the greater majority of hon. members. Therefore, the people living in this municipality will not be treated on an equal footing with the rest of the Canadian people.
In my opinion, once it has been passed by Parliament, an act should apply to the whole of Canada, without consideration of language, race, creed, or province of residence. Because Parliament is the supreme body, such an act should be recognized and adhered to by the whole of Canada. When Bill C-133 was adopted by this House, granting the provinces $250 million with which to improve abandoned or outdated neighbourhoods and develop low

cost housing, we sincerely believed that this legislation would apply universally to the whole of Canada.
This legislation was adopted in June 1973 and it has not yet been implemented in Quebec, while in Ontario, over $36 million have been spent up to now. Mr. Chairman, I think this is not acceptable.
I do not cast any blame on the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) for this, because I know very well who is bluffing in the implementation of this law. The point I want to get across to him is that we, in Quebec, wish to be considered Canadians and respected as all other Canadians; we do not want to be set aside because some government puts peanut politics and autonomy ahead of its citizens way of life.
Mr. Chairman, Bill C-27 comes as the normal and logical sequence of Bill C-133. And because the latter supplements the former, to promote urbanization, mainly in the core of cities such as Winnipeg, Toronto and in small municipalities, this means that if tonight, as member for Lotbiniere, I vote in good faith for the bill, I have to bear in mind that one or two years hence neither Bill C-133 nor Bill C-27 will be implemented in Quebec, and this I cannot accept.
I would like the minister to give me some guarantee tonight that Bill C-133 will bring some advantage to the people of Quebec as much as to those of British Columbia. And I would like him to say what mechanism he provided for in the implementation of Bill C-127 so relocations of railway lines could take place in Quebec, Ontario or Manitoba.
Mr. Chairman, I am not a separatist, I am a Canadian, and proud to be one, but I am sick and tired of voting legislation in this Parliament which has no effect in my own province. I would like the provinces to be consulted before a bill is brought in before Parliament so that when it is passed the bill previously agreed to by all provinces can apply from one coast to the other without distinction.
When under clause 3 the right of a municipality is limited to "acting on behalf of the province", that means- and I draw the minister's attention to that-that the province has a right of veto on the application of this act.
Mr. Chairman, that is not true federalism since any province could decide as it pleased under the opting out rule to withdraw from the legislation voted by the supreme institution that is Parliament. The time that the minister and his officials will have spent implementing or see this legislation through will be time lost.
Mr. Chairman, I would have several questions to put to the minister. What progress has been made in the discussions on Bill C-133 with the province of Quebec? Who is blocking the decisions? The provincial government or the federal government? What relationship is there between Bill C-27 and Bill C-133 and is there any relationship in the setting up of urban planning areas, such as the minister wants, and I congratulate him for that, what guarantee can he give me that Bill C-27 will be more respected in the province of Quebec than Bill C-133? Have there been up to now any discussions or negotiations with any or all of the provinces before this bill was tabled for first reading on April 22 last? Were there discussions with the provinces? If so, what was the provincial response? Did they give
April 29, 1974

their sine qua non agreement? Did they object or did they tell the minister he had their support? What was Quebec's answer on this bill? I would like the minister to put that down in black and white, tonight or tomorrow, to protect me against the Quebec government, who in six months time, for petty reasons of partisan policies, will object to this bill on the grounds of autonomy and small politics.
Mr. Chairman, this is my position. I strongly support this bill since it meets a real need and places at the disposal of our municipalities the money that they need to promote urban development zones. However, because of certain foolish members of our provincial gouvernements, including the Minister responsible for Urban Affairs in Quebec, Quebec will not benefit from this bill and this money. This, Mr. Chairman, is no longer profitable federalism. For my part, I do not believe in politicians, but in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I am counting on the good will of the minister to reassure me and my colleagues on this point. And because I am not confident that the Quebec government will respect the laws of Canada, because I accuse the Bourassa government of being more separatist than the Parti quebecois of Rene Levesque, I say that Premier Bourassa is even more separatist than the separatist party, this is why he does not have my confidence. This is why I would like removed from clause 3 the phrase which says that a municipality will be able to benefit from this biil provided it acts on behalf of the province.
For my part, I say that a municipality that needs federal assistance for the common good should be able to act as far as possible with the agreement of its provincial government. Otherwise, a financial mechanism should be provided to ensure that the municipality will benefit from the assistance, not in a tripartite way, but bilaterally, that is, by the action of the municipal government in association with the federal government.
There is no reason why Victoriaville, Warwick, Prince-ville or my whole riding should be deprived of those amounts of money, when cities like St. Boniface, Sudbury and Hamilton benefit from them. We would be lucky if we had a provincial government that truly believes in Canada, but we do not have that in Quebec, and we too would like to benefit from those advantages. That is why I move the following amendment to clause 3:
That clause 3 of Bill C-27 be amended by deleting the words "on behalf of the province" in line 11 and substituting therefore the words "on its own behalf".
That means, Mr. Chairman, that from now on we are going to build a strong Canada, and make participants of Canadians, municipalities and governments. We are going to make responsible governments of our municipalities and no longer have governments that suffer the unfortunate decisions of some provincial governments. That means, Mr. Chairman, that those of our provincial governments that are not Canadian will have to choose between separatism or reintegrating the ranks of Canadians. Mr. Chairman, the Quebec government which gargles with great literary quotations and autonomy, will have to take advantage of federalism, will have to decide where it belongs in Canada, or else separate. I therefore ask my

colleagues of other provinces to support me in this, in order that all Canadians, from sea to sea, be placed on an equal footing.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate for a brief moment, a number of questions have been forming in my mind as I have listened to it and read those parts which I did not hear. The bill suggests to me that a lot more power will be given to the Canadian Transport Commission. I always thought the Minister of Transport felt that the Commission had much power already and he had none at all. If I am correct in my interpretation of his remarks with regard to transportation in Canada, it is no wonder he is neither taking part in this debate nor in the House listening to it. He probably detests every word of it, seeing more power being given to the CTC and less possibility of a modern transportation system in Canada. Perhaps even a little bit more power is going to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, although I do not see how he enters into the picture other than that he might be the kind of person who can pilot the bill through the House without too much difficulty. The other minister who appears to have some power under the bill is the Minister of Public Works.
As I interpret the amendment put forward by the previous speaker, the onus is upon the municipality to apply for restitution for some kind of improved transportation system. I do not know how many municipalities there are in Canada, but if each one puts forward suggested improvements in the transportation system, we may find ourselves in greater trouble than we are in now, so perhaps we should take a little bit more care to analyse this bill.
Clause 3 (1), of Part I specifically provides "hereinafter in this part called an 'accepted plan'. I looked through the bill to find out what would constitute an "accepted plan", in the eyes of the commission, for an urban transportation development system. I find that the clause goes on to say:
... for that transportation study area, the province or a municipality acting on behalf of the province may, subject to subsection (5) ...
So a municipality may submit what it considers to be an "accepted plan" for a rail grade improvement, a rerouting of present highways to have an overpass on a given railroad or, even, to develop what might be considered as urban transportation within that urban community.
First of all, one should assess what is meant by urban area. In his speech the minister gave the Statistics Canada definition of any area of 30,000 or any community of 1,000 square miles. But that is not the problem facing the major cities across Canada today, Mr. Chairman. They want some kind of study which will determine whether it is feasible for them to develop an urban transportation system within cities with a population of 250,000, 500,000, three-quarters of a million, one million or better. The question is, for which size of city would it be economically feasible to develop an urban transportation system? The bill does not answer that question at all, and I wonder if the Minister of State for Urban Affairs who is piloting this bill through, has an answer. When discussing that part of the bill between clauses 3 and 9, or even 7 and 9, the minister should tell the committee how large those urban areas will be which may qualify for assistance with urban

April 29, 1974
Relocation of Railway Lines
transit systems. I ask the minister to spell out clearly whether he considers an urban transport system economically feasible for cities of one million, 750,000, 500,000, or even 250,000. How big must a place be before it can qualify for aid. So far in this debate he has not told us.
Clause 3 deals with the transportation study area. Is the federal government leaving it to the municipalities to say they need urban transit and is it saying, "We will give you X dollars if you think you can build an urban transit system?" Or, does the federal government intend to establish the same kind of urban transport system for all urban centres of Canada? If so, the government ought to lay down guidelines with regard to criteria and size. I do not want to see happening what I have seen in the United States. In some cities there are, on the same street, streetcars, a trolley bus system, a diesel bus system and, in some cases, a subway system underground. There might even be a monorail system above ground. Under this legislation as drafted, municipalities could set up whatever systems they please. If the system is accepted, they would get a contribution from the government. Which system does the government favour? Is it monorail, the subway, the diesel bus, the trolley bus, or the streetcar which is still plying some streets in Canada.
The government will pay 50 per cent of the cost of a relocation study. How will that affect the CNR? That company, according to the former president, owns 190 choice acres in downtown Toronto. The president could not give the transport committee the value of the land; I suggest that its value is astronomically high.

speechtext: It could be as much as $2 billion.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING, ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Hamilton West suggests it could be worth $2 billion. Perhaps he is right. The government should spell out in the bill the conditions under which it will pay 50 per cent of the cost of the relocation study. I am not overly favourable towards the idea of giving the CNR 190 choice acres in downtown Toronto, which is some of the most valuable real estate in Canada. I am not in favour of my constituents' money being spent to provide the CNR with millions and millions of dollars from the sale or use of land in downtown Toronto.
The bill should be more specific as to what plans will be permitted. Under the bill a certain percentage of the cost of relocation programs will be borne by the government. It is designed to pour oil on troubled waters, in this case the railways, in the hope of placating them. This is a motherhood bill. It even makes provision for railway crossings in small municipalities. If I were not so certain there is not going to be an election I would be inclined to think that this bill has been introduced to foster the hopes and aspirations of many municipal councils, but not to satisfy them.
The bill does not spell out which plans will be accepted. If we are to overhaul the Canadian transport system, we should not overhaul it municipality by municipality or city by city; we should overhaul it from coast to coast. We must overhaul it with a view to improving transportation, not with a view to creating a hodge-podge system, under

which different transport systems will be accepted by different municipalities. That is why I suggest that there should be across Canada one universally accepted mode of urban transit. We do not want to see a monorail system in Toronto, a subway in Montreal, and some other surface system in Edmonton, be that diesel bus, trolley car or streetcar. We want to see the same kind of system serving the entire country, which will make for ease of maintenance and economy of repair.
I suggest the federal government should say, "The same kind of system will operate across the country", instead of saying, "We accept the Toronto plan and system but we do not accept the Edmonton system, and therefore will not help Edmonton." The federal government should lay down criteria for acceptable plans and systems. It should award money according to a points system. If a city meets certain of the requirements, it should score so many points and qualify for a certain level of aid. I think that there should be a limit to the percentage of aid for which one can qualify. I readily concede that it would cost more to build a transit system in a larger centre than in a smaller, that it may cost more to relocate railway lines and build grade crossings in large centres than in small.
I am not enthusiastic about paying the railways 80 per cent of the cost of marking railway cars and locomotives. I think the railways should devise a system for marking their cars clearly so that they are visible by day and by night, but do this without asking the CTC to pay 80 per cent of the cost. In my opinion that would not be proper.
Before we build major urban transit systems, we should study the likely effect of these systems. According to the Financial Post of November 3, about 1.4 billion people in the early 1950's were using some kind of urban transit facility. By 1974 the figure had dropped considerably. In the same period the number of people travelling by car on urban roads had doubled. So, we must assess the effects of any urban transit plan and ask, will the population of a given area support such a plan, and how large must a community be if a plan is to be successful.
I may refer to some of the programs which have already been carried out, within the city of Vancouver the CPR has evacuated a large amount of right of way in that city. A rapid transit system could be developed to bring people from near airport to the centre of Vancouver along that CPR right of way. This minister comes from Vancouver. That is why I draw this to his attention. As of this time, the government has failed to made a proposal, to the province concerning the amount it is prepared to contribute to the cost of an urbanized transit system within that city. Is it 50 per cent or 30 per cent? The government has failed to state what percentage it is prepared to pay.
It is interesting to note that under this bill the government will pay 50 per cent of the cost of a study. As members of parliament, we know how long studies can take. They take as long as politicians and the government wish them to take. If the governments reach a decision, somehow or other the study comes to a close. By the time these studies are completed, the minister may or may not be re-elected. If I were a Vancouver voter, I would want more information before the election. I would want to
April 29, 1974

know what portion of this cost the federal government is prepared to offer the British Columbia government. What portion will the city of Vancouver have to pay?
I have specifically referred to Vancouver. I can also mention Calgary and Edmonton. Both of those cities are attempting to devise an acceptable plan in their eyes for some kind of modernized urban transit system. This bill does not spell out what is, in fact, acceptable. It merely suggests that something acceptable to the province or the municipality on behalf of the province may be accepted. It does not even say will be accepted.
Clause 6 does not set out in detail what is meant by a rapid transit system. It only suggests that it must be rapid. Clause 7 does not say what the government or the railways intend to do with the acquisition of land. I was interested in hearing the minister say this afternoon that the government does not have a ruling on that. I suppose that will also involve some great study.
Clause 9 states that the Minister of Public Works will have the power to dispose of this land in any way he sees fit. I suppose it depends on whether the Department of Public Works goes into the business of providing some kind of rapid transit system.
As far as I am concerned, I do not think the bill is absolutely wrong. However, I suggest the minister must answer a number of very pertinent questions if he wants speedy passage of the bill this evening. No municipality should hold its breath until it gets some funds under this bill because the main purport of the bill is studies first. Mayors and councillors of municipalities will grow gray and long in the tooth before some of the studies this bill purports to involve them in have finally reached a conclusion. I believe the major intent of this bill is to hold out a carrot to those municipalities in dire financial straits in the hope they may think kindly of the present minister. The minister is not taking the city of Vancouver for granted. He is holding out a carrot to them as well as the other cities across Canada.
I wish the minister would set my fears at rest, if not those of others, before we move on to any other clause.
