speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize there are difficulties with this amendment. I have the honour of representing part of the city of Timmins. For a considerable period of time, that city has been concerned with the matter of relocation. Timmins is faced with a problem that is somewhat similar to a problem being faced in Quebec where, if there is going to be anything done, it does not matter if the federal government wants to put up the money. The province wants all the kudos for the money it has expended.
Relocation of Railway Lines
With regard to the relocation of the yards in Timmins, the province is involved in two ways. Because of the British North America Act, the municipality is a creature of the province. Secondly, it is a provincially owned railway. Because of that, the provincial government would be involved in any case.
If this amendment were to pass, it would have the effect of saying that once the federal government agreed to the criteria, they would make the decision as to the advantages of relocation in a particular area. If the provinces and the municipalities agreed with the criteria set by the federal government, that would result in a study. Once those conditions are met, the province would no longer be able to say "no, we will not." The municipality, not in the name of the province but in its own name, would be able to take advantage of the program and the agreement resulting from the criteria set by both the federal and provincial authorities. The municipality would have the final say as to whether the study and relocation would take place.
We have often been plagued, not only in Quebec but also in Ontario, by the fact that the federal government has time and again proven to be totally ineffective and inefficient in providing any type of assistance which would help a large part of the province because the province itself has a designation which strengthens the priority of the province. In my experience, this does not apply to northern Ontario and it has not applied in DREE, ARDA or any of the other federal programs designed to assist the people in norhern Ontario because that has not been the wish of Queens Park.
In the area adjacent to mine in northern Quebec, the problems are very similar. There is a great objection by the province to allowing a municipality or area to take advantage of programs unless the provincial government is given full authority to undertake them. The people mainly affected are those in the municipalities, that is the people directly involved in whatever redevelopment takes place in transportation. After the federal government and the province have made the overall agreement, it is my opinion these people should have a say as to what the criteria will be. The provinces still demand control over programs made available through federal assistance. For example, under the DREE program agreements are made, not with the people who need assistance, but between interested parties in the provinces and their counterparts in the federal government. This system means that very few of the things people in northern Ontario wish to get done are, in fact, accomplished. For many years the people of Timmins have wished to get rid of railroad hazards in their city, to reroute spur lines and, in particular, reconstruct an overpass which creates a dangerous situation since several times a year, when flooding occurs, three or four feet of water covers the road, washing out vehicle transport.
As the hon. member for Crowfoot has pointed out, though, there are certain advantages. Some of us who have been here a long time remember the machinations which took place in Ottawa when it was decided to relocate the rail system of this city. The changes eventually made affected not only Ottawa, but the City of Hull, as well.

April 29, 1974
Relocation of Railway Lines
They meant that a large part of the Province of Quebec could not be served as it had been served by the railway in the past. The National Capital Commission traded off land to the railway, and received land in exchange. The province, it seemed, was in no way concerned with this relocation project.
I do not deny that when new arrangements of this kind are made the consequences of changes brought about by developing an alternative system of transportation must be taken into consideration. But should we not, in keeping with the terms of the British North America Act, reach agreement with the provinces as to the type of program they can implement, or agree to on behalf of their municipalities, and then allow the municipalities to take advantage of the program in their own right without the provinces being called upon to agree to each specific project? It is true that large sums would be required to carry out relocation schemes and rapid transit schemes but on the other hand many of these projects will affect only those who live in the municipality concerned-there will be only a limited effect on the transportation system of the province, and no effect at all on the national transportation picture.
Reading the bill over, I came to the conclusion that the government has been very careful to avoid dealing with the municipalities as powers in their own right. Last week I had the opportunity of attending the annual meeting of the Reeves and Mayors Association attended by representatives of all the municipalities in northeastern Ontario. A general complaint I heard there was to the effect that the municipalities had no say in the implementation of schemes agreed upon between the federal government and the province. Decisions whether or not developments would be carried out in any particular area were made by the province and in any case very little money was usually available for the smaller communities. I suspect this will be true of the relocation proposals. It is all very well for the minister and his officials to word things in such a way that there can be no appeal to the Supreme Court under the British North America Act. This has the effect of making the provinces more powerful and renders less effective efforts by the federal administration to equalize conditions in all parts of Canada in the interest of good order. In the United States laws have been passed by the federal authority in many fields, and such legislation has often been challenged by the state authorities. Very often, the states have lost ground and the federal authority has been able to exercise a much greater influence than it has been possible for the federal government to exercise here.
Like the hon. member who moved this amendment, I come from a part of Ontario which is distressed, which more closely resembles the maritimes than the Golden Horseshoe which controls most of the wealth of Ontario. If we are to have a relocation study and project in the town of Timmins under this legislation we must provide the municipality with the wherewithall to conduct its end of the study because the people with whom they co-operate, and who are at the same time the antagonists, are the agencies of the provincial government. Their aims are not necessarily the same.

You have allowed this amendment, so I presume you agree it is in order. I would strongly urge that we proceed on some other basis than on an archaic interpretation of the British North America Act, because in the past the people in various parts of Canada have not been getting a fair shake from the provincial government. They are only able to take advantage of this kind of legislation to improve their lot if they receive assistance and leadership from the federal government.
I hope the minister will give consideration to this amendment, which in my opinion carries with it the right of the province to set the criteria under which it will participate, as well as giving the federal government the right to set the criteria under which it will participate. Now, in addition, the municipalities will have a say as to whether they will participate in what is to take place. That being so, I hope the minister will see fit to agree that once these criteria are set in accordance with the wishes and desires of the municipalities, this will be sufficient to motivate the passage of this clause which allows these municipalities to participate under federal legislation without the provincial government having a veto.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PLANNING, ACQUISITION OF LAND, GRANTS, GRADE CROSSING ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might just say a word or two about the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lotbiniere. I realize that in the impassioned speech he made there was the suggestion that this legislation be in effect for all provinces, all parts of Canada and all Canadians, and that certainly would be my wish. He asked some specific questions, particularly what was the link between Bill C-133, covering amendments made last fall to the National Housing Act, and this legislation. There is no legislative link as the bills are somewhat different and the procedures are considerably different.
That hon. member in this House and privately expressed his disappointment, which I share, that certain programs under the National Housing Act are not operative in the province of Quebec because the law requires that there be a federal-provincial agreement in order that the programs apply, particularly the neighbourhood improvement program. The housing act says that the program will not apply unless there is federal-provincial agreement, and up until the present time we have been unable to negotiate or finalize an agreement on that matter with the province of Quebec, hence it does not apply there at the present time. This legislation does not make that requirement. It does not say that before this program applies there must be a general federal-provincial agreement. It applies when royal assent is given and the measure is proclaimed.
Part III of the bill, which includes amendments to the grade crossing fund, makes no reference to provinces or provincial approval. The province which the hon. member represents so ably in this House has taken full advantage of the grade crossing fund and the program envisaged in this legislation. For the current year 1974, in the first quarter the province of Quebec has had a commitment from the grade crossing fund in respect of projects within that province amounting to $2.2 million as compared to $1.3 million for the same period in the province of Ontario. So the municipalities in Quebec are now taking very
April 29, 1974

active advantage of the provision relating to grade crossing and grade separation under this legislation.
The hon. member is correct in respect of proposals relative to railroad relocations. Under Section 3 of the act the province, on behalf of a municipality, may apply to the Canadian Transport Commission, submit an urban development or transportation plan and obtain a relocation order from that commission. Regardless of what the constitution may say, it is our obligation as a government to propose legislation which is constitutional, and I think we have endeavoured to observe that obligation.
There are a number of practical reasons that the provinces must be involved in the preparation of urban development plans for presentation to the Canadian Transport Commission. Some of the elements of an urban development plan that would be put before the Canadian Transport Commission will undoubtedly involve such items as municipal goals and objectives, growth forecasts and regional or urban area land uses, and in addition, as one hon. member mentioned this afternoon, questions of environmental and ecological protection. Many of these things are joint responsibilities. Environmental and ecological protection are clearly under provincial responsibility.
Questions of growth and growth strategy are intimately involved with provincial jurisdiction, policies and programs. Unless regional development plans are worked out in close co-operation with the provinces they are not worth anything. They would be prepared in a vacuum if prepared without reference to one of the parties which has most of the power and most of the instruments with which to implement regional development plans.
The Canadian Transport Commission has a clear authority over railways, and clear authority under this legislation to order their relocation, expropriation, and other matters clearly falling within federal jurisdiction. If we are to have regional development plans it is essential that we involve the government which has most of the power and jurisdiction relative to that development, and that is why the section is worded as it is.
I would emphasize that this legislation is not similar to the National Housing Act which in respect of some of its provisions says that before a program can apply there must be an over-all federal-provincial agreement relative to rehabilitation, neighbourhood improvement or land assembly. That is not the case here. In this case we deal on a project by project and proposal by proposal basis. The province of Quebec, in which the hon. member is most interested, although I recognize he was speaking on behalf of municipalities in all provinces, has taken full advantage of the grade crossing provision, and I expect it will take full advantage of the railway relocation proposals. I suggest this is demonstrable by the fact that the city of Quebec has one of the most imaginative ana thoughtful railroad relocation proposals to be presented. It has been worked out and studied in co-operation with my seat mate, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
One of the more interesting proposals is the one in respect of Petite Bourgogne in the city of Montreal. The province of Quebec has agreed to that proposal, as have the residents of that neighbourhood and the federal government. But to relocate and reorganize the railroads in
Relocation of Railway Lines
that area of Montreal would seem to me to be a very silly thing to do unless the provinces, which has much of the jurisdiction in terms of the urban policy, were intimately involved in the preparation of the urban study and urban development plan. Therefore, I think it is essential that the wording of this legislation as proposed be carried.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the logic of the minister's last remarks would fall with thunderous weight on the committee if the minister were addressing himself specifically to the words of the hon. member for Lotbiniere. We all realize that there is a first part to subclause (1) of clause 3, to which apparently the minister is not paying any attention at the moment. Let us look specifically at what the hon. member for Lotbiniere is proposing in his amendment. He is not saying that the province should not be involved in the application of the provisions of this bill; he is not saying that there should be no urban development approved by the municipalities and the provinces jointly; he is not trying to cut out the provinces. All he is trying to do is to allow a little initiative to the municipalities.
Let us look very carefully at the fine, chiselled language of subclause (1) of clause 3, particularly the first part which the minister ignored in his remarks, which reads:
Where, in respect of an area in a province that includes or comprises an urban area (hereinafter in this Part called a "transportation study area"), the government of the province or the municipalities within that area have agreed upon an urban development plan-
Where this is the case, where the government of the province and all municipalities have agreed upon an urban development plan, it goes on to say;
-and transportation plan (hereinafter in this Part called an "accepted plan") for that transportation study area, the province or a municipality acting on behalf of the province may,-
Here is where the hon. member for Lotbiniere suggest that either the province or the municipality may instigate an application. He does not suggest that they carry out a plan which they cooked up by themselves separately, but that they instigate an application for a plan which both entities, the province and the municipalities involved, have worked out together and agreed upon. I say "instigate an application", not carry out a plan because they are still going cap in hand to the Canadian Transport Commission; they do not utter the fiat.
It seems to me that the idea and spirit behind the amendment is a very good one, where two entities, such as the province and the municipality-and this according to the subclause-have agreed upon a plan. You know what that entails-months, probably years of study. When they have agreed upon a plan of development, either one of the entities may instigate an application. Surely, we are not

April 29, 1974
Relocation of Railway Lines
running afoul of the constitution because we are not allowing the municipality or the province to make the final decision; we are leaving it up to the commission which can only act if there has been an agreement between the two entities and a decision.
I like to read the constitution every once in awhile, and I say that this is indeed clearly within the provincial field. There is nothing unconstitutional about the amendment. Let us look at section 92 of the BNA Act, subsection 10 paragraph (a). I will read the whole thing so that we know what the words of section 92 say. It reads:
92. In each Province the Legislature may exclusively make Laws in relation to Matters coming within the Classes of Subjects next hereinafter enumerated ...
Then, you have a list. Under it we find subsection 10 which reads:
Local Works and Undertakings other than such as are the following Classes:-
(a) Lines of Steam of other Ships, Railways Canals, Telegraphs, and other Works and Undertakings connecting the Province with any other or others of the Province, or extending beyond the Limits of the Province;
I know that there are railways in Canada that do not extend from province to province; some operate totally within the province. But the railways with which the hon. member for Lotbiniere is concerned operate from province to province. Most of the railways with which I would be concerned operate from province to province, and certainly would be covered by subsection 10. So I do not think we are violating the constitution. I think that the amendment of the hon. member for Lotbiniere is so well contained and constrained by the extremely thoughtful language which the minister and his minions have put into the bill, it is such a tender little offering to the initiative of municipalities, that we should pass it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the amendment put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin). I support that amendment for two quite specific reasons which greatly concern me as well as the Quebec municipalities which are willing to discharge their duties and their responsibilities towards their ratepayers.
The constitution of our country is a question often referred to, but less during the past few years. Nevertheless, the constitution remains and we must live under three different governments:	federal provincial and
municipal governments.
I would like to mention more particularly the responsibilities of municipal governments. We know that in each municipality, the authorities must do their utmost to assure to ratepayers essential public utilities such as aqueducts, sewers, streets, sidewalks and fire protection. We can even add recreation and other services which municipalities are compelled to provide to ratepayers.
Municipal authorities are complaining, rightly so, that they lack revenue to fulfill their responsibilities, their duties.

Recently, the Canadian Federation of Mayors submitted, in a brief to the cabinet and opposition parties, that the revenues of municipalities are not consistent with their obligations. The Quebec mayors are tired of making representations to the provincial government and always being refused, under the pretext that the province does not have enough money and is unable to bow to their requests.
They have decided to appeal to the federal government for a fair share of tax revenues. That is an indication that municipal administrations want to take their role seriously, to meet their responsibilities without violating the constitution.
On December 6, 1972, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) announced a very specific policy. Under this policy the federal government, in order to help solve the unemployment problem and create jobs, made funds available to the provinces and the municipalities enabling them to do public works likely to create jobs ana ensure services.
On page 2 of this statement, we can read the following: a provincial-municipal fund of $350 million for investment programs for the winter in order to provide provinces and municipalities ...
This is very precise.
... loans and grants for financing investment projects for the winter and the next two years.
And further, Mr. Chairman, the idea which inspired the publication of this statement is precise. On page 6, we can read this:
Each province will have full freedom to administer the amount allocated, including the distribution of funds between the province and its municipalities, and among the municipalities.
... if required.
Should a province prefer not to undertake the administration or distribution, the funds will be made available to the municipalities directly...
Therefore, the object of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) is not to create a precedent.
Therefore, the cabinet then recognized the possibility of funds being made available directly to municipalities. And one can read further:
... subject to the approval of the provincial government.
I agree with that, but I do not agree whenever a government uses its authority to prevent municipalities from taking advantage of federal funds that could help them reach certain objectives while creating employment.
As for me, Mr. Chairman, I am a little fed up of hearing about provincial autonomy and the Constitution, while the development of municipalities and provinces is being crippled through the use of such terms. I would like us to be more up-to-date than that in 1974. There was a time when one could fight for principles. I agree, but since that has been recognized by the people as a whole and the authorities at all levels, I believe we should go ahead.
I keep on with the quotation:
Although the funds are made available to provinces and municipalities, considering the needs and relatively favourable financing condi-
April 29, 1974

tions, it is believed that most of the funds will be in fact assigned to municipalities by provincial governments.
Now, Mr. Chairman, on November 23, 1973, in the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, as one can read in Issue No. 51, I asked the Minister of Finance if he could give us a report on the use of funds in the province of Quebec concerning this program. The minister graciously accepted to table the report on the funds used between December 6, 1972 and October 31, 1973. And in that report, which is public, one can see that out of 43 projects enumerated, the province of Quebec got the lion's share.
The province of Quebec appropriated 70 per cent of the funds for 27 projects, leaving only 30 per cent for all Quebec municipalities which at that date had been able to achieve only 16 projects. I very much regret such a situation, because after all this program was specially designed to help municipalities undertake works that would have created jobs in these centres.
In considering the development plans of the Quebec government, we find that bridges have been built as well as approach works to highways, viaducts, service roads and what not. Furthermore, I would be tempted to believe that these funds have been used for some political purposes on the eve of the provincial election that took place last fall and to fatten the political partisans and the party's servants. We have to call things by their name in such circumstances and be prudent concerning what we are to do in the future.
I would also like to bring another question to the attention of the hon. minister and of this House, that is Bill C-133. Although the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) has just stated that there is no relation between Bill C-27 and Bill C-133, C-27 will however be subordinated, in its application, to the provincial administrators' good will. And it is in the interest of those municipalities that will have set out plans and projects, that the amendment brought forward by the member for Lotbiniere must come into the picture, after the difficulties presently experienced by the federal government with the government of Quebec with regards to the signature of a standard agreement so that the population of Quebec can benefit from this legislation which I have supported because I consider it valuable and because I think it can help municipalities play their role and meet the objectives established by the taxpayers. But, almost a year after the adoption of that legislation, we are still at the negotiating stage and I think that the difficulties must be on the financial side. I suppose that the government of Quebec must ask the federal government: give us the millions, and we will distribute them. I suppose that is where the problem lies.
Mr. Chairman, I agree that the lines of hierarchy must be followed, that the Constitution must be followed, but not that a part of the population has to suffer even though it lives in the province of Quebec. We still want that within Canada, the total wealth of the country serves the whole population independently of where they live.
That is why I would like to ask the minister responsible for Bill C-27 whether he has consulted with the government of the province of Quebec before drafting this bill. If so, could he tell us whether the government of Quebec has given its approval for the adoption of the bill?
Relocation of Railway Lines
If not, does the minister anticipate meeting as humanly as possible the same difficulties he met with Bill C-133?
These are all questions that we can ask ourselves in an objective manner and, believe me, Mr. Chairman, I am asking them in all honesty because I am interested in the municipal field where I spent 30 years of my life. I am probably not as knowledgeabe as the experts, but a bit. This is why I have a right to know the feelings of the authorities of the various municipalities, in the province of Quebec and in the rest of Canada, which really want to go ahead.
We have advocated and we will continue to advocate a solution aimed at helping not only the municipalities, but also the provinces and the federal government, in order to find financing sources which would avoid difficulties. It is in fact a question of money, of income.
I was present at many conferences between the Quebec government and municipalities where they were asking the provincial government to grant them more revenues so that they could meet their responsibilities. The provincial government said: We cannot give you more, the federal government takes everything. It is still the same.
I also attended two federal-provincial conferences where the provincial premiers and ministers of finance told the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner): Give us a larger share of revenues so that we may meet our commitments. And the federal government answered: We do not have enough for ourselves, how can we give you anything?
Mr. Chairman, it is time we changed in depth our financing procedure in the public sector, and serious consideration should be given to our proposal urging a greater use of the bank which belongs to Canadians, the Bank of Canada. This is our institution, and if we must amend the act that governs it, let us start as soon as possible so that the federal government may have a source of financing at a lower cost than at present. This would give the provinces a larger share of revenues. If we could do this, we could eliminate several problems and accomplish many things.
In conclusion, I should like to commend the hon. member for Lotbiniere for moving this amendment designed to foresee, if possible, and prevent a problem like the one that arose with bill C-133. I would also like to ask the minister responsible for Urban Affairs to continue and speed up if possible the negotiations on the subject. If we could obtain a reasonable agreement, it would ensure justice for French Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, while it is not my intention to hold up a committee decision on an amendment moved by the Social Credit Party, if I understood the ruling of the Chair correctly, it appears there is some uncertainty as to whether the amendment is in order. I do not know therefore, whether I would be assisting the Chair by discussing clause 3 until ten o'clock, in which case the Chair would have until tomorrow to decide whether the amendment was in order. If I am wrong in my assumption, Mr. Chairman, please correct me.

April 29, 1974
Relocation of Railway Lines
Assuming that my interpretation is correct, I wonder if I could outline again some of my problems. I assume that the moneys set out in the recommendations are the total moneys allocated for a single project, not the total moneys allocated for all projects under the specific definition. If the minister believes I am wrong in this, I encourage him to correct me.
If I am correct in this, then there is no end to the amount of money available in a given situation, specifically in the studies proposed, specifically the relocation grants, specifically the painting of boxcars and engines- the whole list of possibilities where moneys may be allocated to municipalities or railroads. If this is the case, could the minister give the House an explanation as to why the government did not feel it necessary to specify the criteria so that we could be assured there was no partisanship on the part of the three ministers involved, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, the Minister of Transport, or even the CTC?
This question is prompted by the example of the LIP program. The riding of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs received seven times more LIP money than a riding in Vancouver which is adjacent to his. What criteria were used? Under the LIP program a certain amount of money was allocated to Canada as a whole and lists of projects were compiled. Yet, in a city comprised of six or seven ridings, the minister's riding received seven times the amount allocated to the riding represented by one or other of the opposition parties.
If I am correct in my interpretation of the regulations for this bill, there is no limit on the amount of money but there is an "accepted plan". It is spelled out very clearly in line 11, page 3, in Part I, clause 3, and again in subclause (5) on page 4, line 8, which reads:
Where an application to the Commission under subsection (1) is made in respect of an accepted plan that contemplates the use of federal programs ...
In view of the partisanship shown by the minister and the cabinet, the committee should be told what constitutes an accepted plan. For instance, the CPR has removed certain tracks in the Vancouver area. Will the federal government give the city of Vancouver money with which to buy that right of way from the CPR? Or, will Saskatoon be reimbursed for its previous purchase of CNR right of way? Will retroactive actions be considered, or will the bill apply only to plans which will be carried out in future? The minister has remained silent on that aspect. The subclause provides that the urban development or transportation plans shall not be received by the commission unless it is shown to the commission that, as clause 3(5)(a) says:
(a) the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is satisfied that the federal programs contemplated for use in the urban development plan forming part of the accepted plan are available and would contribute significantly to the improvement of any urban area within the transportation study area in respect of which the application is made;...
According to the bill, the government will pay not more than 50 per cent of the amount of the cost of preparing urban development plans and transportation plans. Such plans, as I have mentioned just now, must contribute

significantly to the improvement of an urban area. What criteria will be used to determine if a plan contributes significantly? Will there be environmental considerations? For instance, carrying out a plan might mean that the CPR will not pollute the Fraser Valley with coal dust from coal cars. What will be a significant contribution? I can imagine many transportation studies, particularly in the Vancouver area, which would contribute significantly to improving the urban area in respect of which the application is made. I am not a lawyer, but I suggest that "significant" could mean more than 50 per cent in this case.
I remember in the debate on the farm marketing bill the minister of agriculture of that time said, "significant" means more than 10 per cent of a certain figure. I do not know what the words, "contributes significantly to the improvement of any urban area within the transportation study area" mean. The minister should explain the criteria which the government will apply. For instance, will the federal government accept transportation studies into which it has had no input but towards the cost of which it is expected to pay. Further, will the federal government in some cases pay 50 per cent of the cost of relocating tracks; will it, in other cases, contribute only, say, 37 per cent of the cost, or 25 per cent?
I know that both Edmonton and Calgary are studying urban transport. Once the bill is passed, can they apply to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and say, "Our transportation study was not comprehensive enough. As the government is paying 50 per cent of the cost, we want to do a new, more comprehensive study, which will cover our needs for the next 20 or 30 years; our current study covers a much shorter period." The minister should spell out clearly what is meant by transportation study. Will 50 per cent of the sort of study I have just mentioned be covered? Once a transportation study for a certain area is approved, will the federal government automatically pay a portion of the cost of such study?
The minister does not seem willing to rise in his place and answer. He seems reluctant to speak. I notice the Minister of the Environment moving over to converse with him. That minister was involved in a transportation study involving the Vancouver area which created all sorts of pollution, so to speak, in that area. The interests of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and The Minister of Transport conflicted. In the result, coal coming from the interior of British Columbia and Alberta could not be unloaded at Squamish even though the natural harbour was ideally suited for the handling of coal. Because of the conflicting interests of three ministers, and their embarrassment and indecision, the greater Vancouver area suffered a loss. May I call it ten o'clock?
Progress reported.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-STATUS OF PROPOSED PASSENGER HEAD TAX
AIR TRANSPORT-STATUS OF PROPOSED PASSENGER HEAD TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago, like many other members of this House, I was rather curious as to what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the department were doing with the proposed airport head tax on passengers. Accordingly, I asked the minister what I thought were a couple of reasonable and sensible questions as to why there were delays, and what was now the status of the tax. I received a very unsatisfactory response, which is why I wanted to bring the matter forward for debate this evening. The Department of Transport has been so kicked around lately that one almost feels sorry for having to say anything more about it. I guess everything has been said that can be said. However, even with a situation like this, it has to be pointed out that if there ever was a do-nothing department, it has to be this one, at least at the present time.
How can the Minister of Transport and the department seriously purport to be working on a meaningful transport policy for this country when they cannot even bring forward an administrative measure that was proposed with great fanfare last December? How can the department under present conditions, do an efficient job of providing
Adjournment Debate
Canadians with efficient transport when a matter as routine as a proposed airport head tax cannot be resolved, explained or apparently dealt with in definitive fashion? As far as this tax is concerned, we on this side of the House are not convinced it should be implemented at all, but having brought the measure foward with such great fanfare, and having done so in a very tactless and bumbling manner, at least after this many months the situation should be clarified.
Just how bad the minister's timing and sense of propriety was is illustrated in the proceedings of the standing committee for last December 6. At that time I had occasion to question Mr. Pratte of Air Canada. After a bit of preamble, we discussed the imposition of the tax and the announcement, about which he knew nothing until he had it reported to him or read it in the paper. I said, and I quote:
Well, Mr. Pratte, I do not know how you feel about the situation, and I do not want to be unfair to you or express feelings that I have no business expressing, but I am indignant on your behalf, that you, as President of our national airline, had to learn from very indirect sources of this type of major decision that is going to affect you and so many of your employees.
Is this the type of thing that you are reported as expressing dissatisfaction about in the past? Are you satisfied that there is sufficient communication between yourself and the Ministry of Transport not only out of ordinary business courtesy but so your airline and your top management can prepare most efficiently and most directly for this sort of thing? Are you happy with this situation?
Mr. Pratte replied:
In that particular case I thought there should have been more consultation not only with Air Canada but with industry generally. You know, all carriers relatively speaking are going to be hit to the same extent as we are, except that in our case since we have a greater proportion of short-haul passengers than others this is probably going to hurt us more than it would a long-haul carrier due to the fact that the tax is on a per-passenger basis.
Mr. Pratte and Mr. Baldwin then went on to illustrate just how terrible communications were and how ill conceived, bumbling and lucicrous the minister's attempts to that point were to implement this administrative measure. I said to Mr. Baldwin:
So I suppose not only will you have the fare increase that you were proposing to have but the administrative details and complications involved in this will result in a larger fare increase than you otherwise had planned.
Mr. Baldwin replied:
Well, we will have to recover, if we move in this direction, not only the amount to be paid to the government but there will be added administrative costs within the airline in terms of procedures and staff work.
The dialogue goes on and on. I do not want to take the time of the House to illustrate how terrible and ridiculous this situation is at present. Now, after months and months of questions, we find that the minister is continuing to make a complete fiasco out of this affair as he has done with so much of his department's administration. He succeeded in alarming the Canadian public, the domestic air transport industry, in alienating the international aviation organizations to which Canada belongs, IATO and ICAO, and, most of all, in refusing to clarify what is going on. Now, he adds to the confusion by saying the matter is being discussed within the department. At least the department is finally being given a voice, but why was this not done last December?

April 29, 1974
Adjournment Debate
When the people of Canada and the industry continue to expect something which they should know better than to expect from this government and this minister, why does the government continue to indicate it is not prepared to give us any answers? I believe the minister said to me, when I asked him a question on April 22: "If we were in a position to give all those details the matter would not be under discussion in the department; it would have been discussed." I say to the government and to its spokesman tonight: Is it not high time that this matter was discussed and that this do-nothing department brought forward a definitive policy? It is perhaps too much to ask them to produce a general policy, but could they not give us some indication of the proposal which will be produced to implement this tax? Will they go ahead with it or will they withdraw in their usual confusion? Do they know? That is my question, tonight.

do-nothing policy, but it is the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) who wants to impose a tax on the people a lot earlier than it might otherwise be imposed, as a result of his insistence. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-STATUS OF PROPOSED PASSENGER HEAD TAX
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is correct.
A final decision has not yet been made by the government in respect of either the airport fee which was announced in December 1973 or any other of the various alternatives which could be implemented as a means of generating the same amount of additional revenues.
However, I can confirm that the Air Transportation Tax Act, which all hon. members will recall was passed by parliament in December, 1969, appears to be the preferred measure, at least as viewed by the Air Transportation Association of Canada, the Air Transport Association of the United States, the International Air Transport Association and the air carriers.
I wish to assure the House that very careful consideration is being given to all factors associated with additional cost recovery policies in the Ministry of Transport, not only to determine measures which are administratively feasible but, more important, measures which are economically and socially desirable. For example, special attention must be given to the circumstances of people living in the more remote areas of Canada in terms of providing transportation to them at a cost which will not result in discrimination simply on the ground that they live too far away from the major metropolitan areas of Canada which are serviced, for example, by big, international airports with their related sophisticated air services.
We must also pay particular attention to some of the harsh realities in respect to air transportation in Canada, and one of these is that air transportation cost per seat-mile is significantly higher in the northern parts of

Canada as compared with the more southerly parts. We are examining ways to make sure that any additional cost recovery measures will not impose undue hardship in the north while at the same time maintaining the principle of equity between all users of air transportation services and facilities in Canada.
As hon. members are aware, the Air Transportation Tax Act provides for a per cent ad valorem rate to be levied on the price of air tickets paid, or payable, in Canada. Anyone can appreciate that such a tax could result in additional costs of about $18 on a return air journey from St. John's to Vancouver. All members could easily work out further illustrations by applying a 5 per cent rate to the price of various air tickets. This unlimited application of a percentage rate has been causing some concern and we are seeking solutions to this problem.
I am grateful to members of this House for having made various suggestions to the minister over the last several months and these suggestions together with all other factors which have been brought to our attention, keeping in mind that our officials have been conducting extensive consultations with the air industry associations, the carriers and the public, will be evaluated in order to allow the government an opportunity to make a decision based on all relevant information.
Speaking personally again, I for one would not at the moment wish to impose that tax as I always feel these taxes come too soon.

subtopic: PENSIONS-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE GREATER PROTECTION AND ESCALATION FOR PERSONS IN PRIVATE PLAN
PENSIONS-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE GREATER PROTECTION AND ESCALATION FOR PERSONS IN PRIVATE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday March 21, as recorded in Hansard at page 727, I put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) the first part of which was in these words:
Is the government giving consideration to making amendments to the Pension Benefits Standards Act or to introducing any other legislation to provide greater protection for those who are enrolled in private pension plans?
That was the main thrust of my question put in general terms. The fact is that I am concerned about the many ways in which those who are in private pension plans need greater protection. Then I went on to put a specific question. I stated it twice, but perhaps I may quote it tonight in the words I used when I got to my feet the second time. I put it in this way: will the minister:
-take steps to provide in the legislation that all private pension plans must escalate their pensions, during the years of retirement, according to the rise in the cost of living?
As I have already indicated in raising this question, I am concerned in a general way about the protection needed by persons in private pensions plans. They need protection to make sure that the funds are there, that the pensions they are supposed to get will be payable to them when the time of retirement comes and so on. But the grievance which is being felt most strongly these days by recipients of pen-
April 29, 1974

sions from private plans has to do with the matter of escalation.
The government has done fairly well, with a little prodding from some of the rest of us in Parliament, in providing annual escalation on a cost of living basis for just about all pensions that come under federal government responsibility, but private plans are lagging very much in this respect, and it does seem to me that the time has come for the government to make it clear that private pension plans ought to follow suit.
Late in 1973 the income tax regulations were amended to permit private pension plans to escalate to the full extent of the cost of living, not just 2 per cent as had previously been the case, and still get income tax deductibility, but that is all the government has done thus far. It has just put this on a permissive basis. There is the Pension Benefits Standards Act which controls and regulates pensions that come under federal responsibility. I think the time has come for the Pension Benefits Standards Act to say that all pensions that come under federal jurisdiction or responsibility should be required to be escalated after retirement by the full amount of the cost of living.
Let me give an example, and I mention it not because I generally think that banks are bad boys but because they are an example that comes to mind. Let me give the example of chartered banks. Many of them have reached the point where they are providing some escalation of the pensions of their retired employees. In most cases it is a 2 per cent escalation or an ad hoc amount; in very few cases is it an escalation equal to the actual rise in the cost of living. But what really concerns and annoys some retired bank employees who have been in touch with me is that when a bank provides an escalation in the pension of a retired employee, it does so subject to that escalation being cut back when there is an escalation of old age security. So the whole idea of pensioners getting an escalation in their income so that they can keep up with the cost of living is nullified when a pensioner gets an escalation in one pension but has his other pension cut back by that same amount. He ends exactly where he started. I say to you, sir, that that is actually happening in the case of some chartered banks in this country with respect to their retired employees. Banks do come under the Pension Benefits Standards Act. They are under the jurisdiction and responsibility of the federal government.
I suppose I should simply say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that I hope he will have a talk with some of these banks and help them to see the light with respect to this matter. But so far as I can tell from other talks that he has had, not a great deal has resulted from them and I think the time has come for something more than talk. That is why I urge legislation to protect those in private pension plans and in particular to protect their right to escalation of pensions and their right not to have their escalation nullified in the way that it is now being done in so many cases.

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PENSIONS-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE GREATER PROTECTION AND ESCALATION FOR PERSONS IN PRIVATE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising in connection with the inquiry from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who wanted to know wheth-
Adjournment Debate
er the government would introduce a piece of legislation to force private pension plans to escalate their benefits during retirement years in line with the rise in the cost of living index. I should like to make a few remarks concerning the federal and provincial legislation in this area.
Let us not forget, when we receive inquiries such as this, that the federal government is empowered to act only in connection with pension plans in areas of employment under the jurisdiction of Parliament, as listed in the Schedule to the Pension Benefits Standards Act.
Most pension plans for workers in Canada come under the jurisdiction of the provinces, four of which have adopted provisions similar to those in the Pension Benefits Standards Act.
The only way whereby the federal government could try to obtain the escalation of pension benefits in all pension plans would be indirectly, through the Income Tax Act. Normal penalty for violations of this requirement could then be a withdrawal of registration in tne plan, which would prevent both employer and employee contributions from being deductible under income tax legislation. The end result for employees could be still lesser protection of their future than they now enjoy.
Any federal action in this direction would materially alter the agreed roles of the two levels of government under federal and provincial pension plans that have come into being during the last ten years, in order to improve on private employers' pension plan transferability and solvency.
None of these legislations force employers to offer pension plans, nor prevents them from ending plans, considering employers had enough difficulty in financing pension plans without benefit escalation, such a requirement could very well force employers into terminating existing plans. Hon. members will no doubt understand that such measures can only be envisaged with utmost caution.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INCREASE IN CORPORATE PROFITS AND DECREASE IN LABOUR'S SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME-GOVERNMENT ACTION
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INCREASE IN CORPORATE PROFITS AND DECREASE IN LABOUR'S SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 15, as recorded at page 1415 of Hansard, I asked two questions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).
The first dealt with the fact that the labour component of the national income in Canada had fallen to 70 per cent from 75 per cent, while the corporate share of our national income had risen in the same period by approximately the same number of points, that is, by 5.3 points to 12 per cent of our national income. Here I am referring to the corporate profit after tax.
Then, not being satisfied with my first answer I asked the minister a second question, as to whether or not he was aware of the fact that in Canada corporate profits were running at "12 per cent of total Canadian income compared to 6.6 per cent for corporations in the USA." I asked him:
-does the minister still believe it is necessary to continue his liberal tax concessions to Canadian corporations bearing in mind such

April 29, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Canadian corporations now earn more after tax than American companies earn before tax in relation to national incomes?
I raise this question because I feel that it is dramatically shown, in the figures now coming out of the various statistical agencies, that there has been a very deliberate shift on the part of the government with respect to the sharing of national income in Canada.
Since replying to those questions in the House the minister had an opportunity to speak in Winnipeg on April 19, to which speech I wish to make reference, and today we were furnished with the Economic Review dated April, 1974, from the minister's department. I find this review extremely interesting because at pages 52 and 53, in effect, the minister confirms the point that I had raised. Here I refer to the fact that he says, according to page 52, that the "before-tax profits accounted for a larger share of the nation's gross income in 1973 than the average since 1958." I am disappointed that in making that reference the minister was not more explicit and did not refer to the actual figures.
In his answer to me on April 15 he indicated that he could show that my figures were reversed in the previous decade. At that time I indicated that that was not so, and I reiterate it tonight.
At page 53 of the Economic Review which came out today, the minister says:
In 1973, wages, salaries and supplementary labour income was down to 70 per cent-
That is actually the figure I had used.
-of net national income-
He then says:
Thus in real terms, average increases in labour income per employee or in wages and salaries increased very little or actually fell in 1973.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize that I believe the minister has been most unfair to the people of Canada and to this House in referring, from time to time, to real disposable income for the average Canadian going up 6.8 per cent in 1973. I say this because it was known privately, that the minister could only justify that figure by using a deflator which has rarely been used up until now by statisticians as opposed to using the customary consumer price index deflator. I hope that the minister will explain this to the House. I am pleased that in his review tabled today he at least shows the two deflators in action. They point out, Mr. Speaker, that if the Consumer Price Index deflator is used Canada's real growth was 4.8 per cent in 1973, not 6.8 per cent, which is the figure that the minister has bandied around for some time. If you use the CPI deflator, the effect is shown in the review at page 53 where it is pointed out that the average workman's wages have actually decreased by .9 per cent.
I mention this because I hope that the parliamentary secretary will explain to the House why they have chosen to evade my question when it was put in the House and subsequently to use a deflater, which I feel is not relative, when the minister spoke in Winnipeg.
There is a footnote on page 52 explaining the difference between the CPI deflator and what is generally known as the consumption inflator. I find the minister's suggestion truly remarkable. He states that he thinks it is preferable to use the consumer deflater in that it does not allow for shifts by consumers toward less expensive goods and services as price structures change.
In plain English the minister is saying that inflation in this country has become so devastating that people are having to give up good food and shift to less expensive food. Then, the government has the colossal gall to come to this House and indicate that it wants to use the deflator to show that the lower costs are in truth there because people are giving up the better quality foods in order to eat the less expensive. This is a very, very sad testimony of the mismanagement of this government in our economic affairs. In short, they are saying, "if you cannot eat beef, turn to spaghetti and macaroni or any other cheap food and we will use a deflator to make the over-all economic performance look better". I hope we have an explanation of this tonight, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INCREASE IN CORPORATE PROFITS AND DECREASE IN LABOUR'S SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member states that in the past three years, profits after taxes have jumped over 5 points of national income while the labour share of the national income has declined 5 points.
The published data do not indicate such a substantial alteration as suggested by the hon. member. In 1973, the profits share was 3.8 points higher than in 1970 and the labour share was lower by 2.8 points.
In percentage of the net national income in relation to cost factors, I would like to quote a few figures for the average period extending from 1965 to 1973: profits after taxes, 9 per cent and labour income, 70.9 per cent. The average for 1970-73 is 8.8 per cent and 72 per cent. For 1969, it was 8.4 and 71.2 per cent; for 1970, 7.3 and 72.8; for 197l'
7.9	and 72.9; for 1972, 9 and 72.2; for 1973, 11.1 and 70 per cent. The difference between 1969 and 1973 is 2.7 for benefits after taxes and 1.2 per cent for labour income. From 1970 to 1973, there was a difference of 3.8 per cent and -2.8 per cent.
The years chosen by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) give a highly exaggerated idea of the evolution, 1970 having been characterized by an exceptionally low rate of profits, and unusually high income. In 1973, profits were 2.1 per cent lower than the average for the period 1965-73, while the percentage corresponding to salaries were 0.9 lower than the average. In fact, profits as a percentage of the GNP were lower in 1970, shares reaching their lowest level since 1949.

April 29, 1974

It is true that profits, before and after taxes, were higher than usual in 1973. Before tax deductions, they amounted to more than $14.5 billion, that is 12.5 per cent of the GNP. Profits after tax deductions were slightly more than $10 billion. Still, it must be noted that companies did not increase their dividends by much in 1973. The greater part of their additional profits were kept to finance investments, and retained earnings amounted to $7.8 billion that
Adjournment Debate
year. Those retained earnings, added to depreciation amounting to $6.5 billion, provided $14.3 billion in cash flow for investing. In 1974, businesses expect to invest $18.5 billion in Canada. As the minister said in reply to the hon. member, those investments will mean more production, employment and income for all Canadian workers.
